t: Passage planning: the 4 stages, a checklist and a template
d: What a passage plan is, the four stages, how to make one step by step, a template and a worked example for a motor yacht. Plus how we review or write yours.
x: What is passage planning, and is it the same as voyage planning? The 4 stages of passage planning How to make a passage plan, step by step 1. The season 2. The weather window 3. Your boat's real range 4. Entrances and arrival times 5. Ports of refuge 6. Charts, pilots and paper backup 7. Entry, exit and paperwork 8. Crew, watches and rest 9. Safety gear and drills 10. Communications and shore contact 11. Boat readiness 12. The alternative plan Passage plan template Passage plan example: Gold Coast to Sydney Passage planning apps and software What we do What is a passage plan? What are the 4 steps of passage planning? What is the difference between voyage planning and passage planning? Do I legally need a passage plan on a private motor yacht? Is there a passage plan template or example I can use? Can you review or write a passage plan for me? A passage plan is a written plan for getting your boat from one place to another safely, and the part people forget is the last bit: what will we do when it does not go to plan? Anyone can draw a line between two ports. The plan is everything around the line: the weather window, the fuel, the way in, the way out, who is aboard and who ashore knows where you are. It works the same off the Gold Coast, across the Tasman or in the Mediterranean; only the details change. Key facts - What it is — a written plan for the whole trip, berth to berth, with alternatives - The 4 steps — appraisal, planning, execution, monitoring (IMO Resolution A.893(21)) - The rule — SOLAS V/34 requires voyage planning; how it applies to a private yacht depends on your flag - The test — a plan is only good if it tells you what to do when conditions change - Our offer — we review the plan you have, or write it for you What is passage planning, and is it the same as voyage planning? Passage planning is the job of working out, before you leave, how the trip will be done safely. SOLAS Chapter V, Regulation 34 calls it voyage planning and says the master must plan the intended voyage on appropriate charts and publications before going to sea. Port State Control guidance describes the result as a berth-to-berth plan. Yachting courses and clubs usually say passage planning. In practice they are the same job: a plan for the whole trip, from the moment you leave the berth to the moment you are alongside at the other end. Whether the law requires one for a private yacht depends on the flag and where you are, so check yours. The reason to do it anyway is simpler. A plan made calmly on the dock is better than decisions made tired, offshore, with a deadline. The 4 stages of passage planning The IMO’s guidelines for voyage planning, Resolution A.893(21), break the job into four parts. Use them as the spine of your own plan, however big the boat. Appraisal. Gather everything: charts, pilot books, weather patterns for the season, port and entry information, the boat's limits, the crew's experience. Planning. Draw the route and the alternatives. Work out distances, speeds, fuel, tides, daylight arrivals and ports of refuge. Execution. Brief the crew, check the latest weather, confirm the boat is ready, and leave on the plan, not on the day you hoped for. Monitoring. Check position, fuel and weather against the plan every watch, and change the plan early when they drift apart. What a plotted passage looks like — waypoints, course and distance for each leg, the current, the area to avoid and the way out. An illustration, not a real chart. How to make a passage plan, step by step Twelve things to settle before you leave any port. This is the appraisal and planning stages in the order we work through them. 1. The season The same route can be easy in one month and dangerous in the next. Every ocean basin has its own tropical cyclone season, monsoon and swell pattern. Find out the season for each leg, not just the departure port, and plan to be somewhere safe when the bad months start. The US National Hurricane Center’s Mariner’s Guide has a chapter on tropical cyclone seasons by basin that is a good place to begin. 2. The weather window Pick the window from the forecast, not the calendar. Look at wind, swell height and period, and above all wind against current or against swell, which turns a modest sea steep and short. Decide your go and no-go limits for this boat and this crew before the pressure of a departure date is on you. Re-check right up to the lines coming off. 3. Your boat’s real range Brochure range is not passage range. Work out fuel from your own burn at your planned speed, then add a reserve. Rough weather, a dirty hull, a head current or a forced diversion all cost fuel. Know the longest leg between fuel, and whether you can reach a port of refuge from the middle of it. Our fuel cost guide shows how burn changes with speed. 4. Entrances and arrival times Many harbours are easy in daylight and on the right tide and hazardous in the dark or on the ebb. Check every entrance for bar conditions, depth at low water, tidal streams, restrictions and the hours you can enter. Plan to arrive in daylight with margin. A late arrival that forces a night entrance into a strange harbour is the plan failing, not bad luck. 5. Ports of refuge For each leg, list where you can duck in if the weather turns or something breaks, and how far away that is at the middle and the far end of the leg. If the answer is “nowhere for 200 miles”, that is a decision to make deliberately, with extra fuel and spares, not a surprise. 6. Charts, pilots and paper backup Carry up-to-date electronic and paper charts for the whole route, plus the pilot books or sailing directions. Electronic charts fail, and remote regions often have poor or old survey data. Treat unsurveyed or old-survey areas with extra margin, and keep a paper plot of your route. 7. Entry, exit and paperwork Every country has its own rules for arrival: clearance, customs, immigration, biosecurity, cruising permits and agents. Some require notice before you arrive, and some ports of entry are far apart. Start this early. Flag, registration, crew passports and visas, insurance certificates and the boat’s papers all need to be current and on board. 8. Crew, watches and rest Count the people, the qualifications and the rest. A passage plan should say who keeps which watch, who is the second person who can run the boat, and when the skipper actually sleeps. Tired crews make the mistakes that end passages. Cowes Harbour’s passage-planning notice lists the condition of the crew alongside weather and tide as something to plan for. Crew and watches — who is at the helm, who relieves them and when the skipper sleeps belong in the plan. 9. Safety gear and drills Lifejackets, liferaft, EPIRB or PLB, flares, fire gear, bilge pumps, medical kit and spares are all checked against the length and remoteness of the trip, not a minimum. Brief the crew on where things are and who does what in a man-overboard, a fire and a flooding. Insurers often care about all of it. 10. Communications and shore contact Have more than one way to talk and get weather offshore: VHF, satellite voice or messaging, and a backup. Leave a written plan with someone ashore: route, dates, boat and crew details, check-in times and what to do if you miss one. AMSA’s guidance for boaters starts with exactly this: plan your trip and tell someone where you are going. 11. Boat readiness Before a long passage the boat itself needs checking: engines and fluids, filters, generator, steering, stabilisers, batteries, bilges, anchors, and the hull and running gear. A pre-departure service and a short sea trial find problems at the dock, where they are cheap, rather than offshore, where they are not. 12. The alternative plan Write down what you will do if the weather window shuts, if a mechanical fault appears, if someone is injured or if a port is closed to you. Include who to call and the decision points where you will turn back or divert. This page of the plan is the one you hope never to use and are glad to have. Worth knowing Planning is not a one-off document. The monitoring stage means comparing position, fuel and weather with the plan every watch and updating it when they diverge. The best plans on paper are the ones that get changed early. Execution — the lines come off on the plan, not on the day you hoped for. {{cta}} Passage plan template Copy these headings into a document or a notebook. One row per leg, plus the whole-trip items at the bottom. Item What to write Boat Name, flag, length, draft, air draft, fuel capacity, cruising speed and burn Crew Names, roles, qualifications, watch roster, emergency contacts Route Departure port, each waypoint, arrival port, total distance Each leg Distance, planned speed, time, tides and currents, daylight or dark arrival Entrances Bar, depth at low water, tide window, restrictions, VHF channel Weather Forecast sources, go limits, no-go limits, date and time checked Fuel Burn per hour, fuel per leg, reserve, where you can refuel Refuge Ports of refuge for each leg, and the distance to each Paperwork Clearance, permits, agents, certificates, insurance Communications Radio, satellite, check-in times, who is ashore and their number If it goes wrong Decision points, diversion options, who to call Passage plan example: Gold Coast to Sydney {{map:gold-coast-to-sydney}} This is a short worked example in the same headings. The figures come from our Gold Coast to Sydney guide , which has the sources. Item Example entry Route Gold Coast Seaway to Sydney Harbour, about 470 nautical miles Legs Seaway to Coffs Harbour (about 150 nm), Coffs to Port Stephens (about 160 nm, the longest), Port Stephens to Sydney (85 to 110 nm) Entrances Sydney, Newcastle and Port Stephens have no bar. Ballina, Yamba, Port Macquarie, Camden Haven, Forster and Swansea are designated bars: incoming tide only, lifejackets on Weather Avoid southerly changes against the south-setting East Australian Current; leave the Seaway at first light on the flood Fuel Plan Coffs as an overnight stop, not a fuel stop; top up at Newcastle or Port Stephens Refuge Yamba and Forster in reserve to shorten a leg Shore contact Log on with Marine Rescue NSW by VHF 16, with destination, people aboard and expected arrival Passage planning apps and software Charts and weather now live in apps and on the chartplotter, which makes plans easier to draw. They do not make them for you. An app will draw the line and add up the distance. It will not tell you whether the entrance is safe on the ebb, whether your crew is rested, or where you go if the fuel computes short. Use the tools for the arithmetic and keep the judgement on paper. What we do A lot of owners and captains have a plan in their head and a route on the chartplotter, and want someone experienced to look at it before the lines come off. That is what we do. Passage plan review. You send us your route, dates, boat details and crew. We go through it line by line and tell you what is missing, what is risky and what we would change. A second pair of eyes before a long crossing. Passage plan build. We write the full plan for you: route and alternatives, weather windows, fuel and range, ports of refuge, entry paperwork, crew and watch plan, and emergency procedures. Support while you are under way. Weather routing and shore support for an owner or captain making the crossing themselves, or our own delivery crew aboard to take her there. We plan and support passages from the Gold Coast, Sydney and the Whitsundays, and further afield across the Pacific. The fee depends on the passage and how much of the work you want, so we quote each one. Call 0439 748 387 or email yachtsupport@marinehq.com.au with your route and dates. {{product:checklists}}

t: Pre-purchase boat inspection: what to check and what a survey costs
d: How to inspect a motor yacht before you buy: what you check yourself, what a marine surveyor does and costs in Australia, the red flags, and when to call in a specialist.
x: Inspection, survey and sea trial: three different jobs What to check yourself first Red flags What a surveyor does What a survey costs in Australia When to call a surveyor, and when to call someone else How we help After you buy How much does a pre-purchase boat survey cost in Australia? What is the difference between a survey, a sea trial and an inspection? Can I use the seller's or broker's surveyor? Who pays for the lift-out? Does a surveyor check the engines? What if the seller will not allow a survey or sea trial? Is a pre-purchase survey the same as an insurance survey? Do your own inspection first, then hire an independent marine surveyor, then run a sea trial before you sign. The inspection costs you a morning and tells you whether the boat deserves a survey. The survey is the report that lets you walk away or renegotiate. On the Gold Coast, published pre-purchase survey rates for a 50 to 59 ft motor yacht run from about $1,500 to $1,600 before extras, which is a small amount against what a bad purchase costs. Key facts - Three different things — your own walk-through, the surveyor’s report, and the sea trial - Survey, 50 to 55 ft — $1,499 at Maritime Surveyor; 50 to 59 ft $1,600 at BoatBuy, plus $210 per engine - Quoted on application — from 56 ft at Maritime Surveyor, from 60 ft at BoatBuy - Extras — lift-out (the yard bills it), generators $210 each, oil analysis $185 to $199 a sample - Registration — transfer into your name within 14 days; at 15 m or longer Maritime Safety Queensland must endorse it - Independent — appoint your own surveyor, not the seller’s or broker’s Inspection, survey and sea trial: three different jobs People use these words as if they meant the same thing. They do not. Your own inspection. A walk-through with a torch, a checklist and the paperwork. It costs nothing and its job is to eliminate boats. If she fails here, you have saved a survey fee. The survey. A surveyor's written report on the whole vessel, usually with photographs. Nearly everything is inspected, covers are unscrewed and the items that could not be reached are listed as not inspected. A small patch of antifoul is removed so the surveyor can take moisture readings on a fibreglass hull. The sea trial. A test run, usually part of the survey, that shows how she steers, trims and performs under load. It can reveal handling problems, steering or trim issues and thrusters that are too small or cavitate. It has to be agreed in advance with the seller and the surveyor. A pre-purchase survey is not an insurance survey. An insurance survey is shorter, covers the main items that decide seaworthiness and does not need a sea trial. A full pre-purchase report can often do both jobs, which is why it is the one to buy first. Check with your insurer that they will accept it. What to check yourself first Do this before you pay anyone. A boat in this class, a 40 to 120 ft Sunseeker, Azimut, Pershing or Princess, comes with long service histories, and the paperwork often tells you more than the hull does. The paperwork. - Registration and ownership. Check that the seller is the registered owner and that the registration is current. Queensland lets you check a boat’s registration online, through the Rego Check app or on 13 23 80. - Finance owing. A financier records its interest in a boat on the Personal Property Securities Register, and a search on the hull identification number shows it. Boatsonline puts that search at about $2. A boat with a security interest registered can be repossessed, so ask for the payout and discharge in writing. - Certificate of currency and claims history. A current certificate and a straight answer about past claims, groundings and repairs. - Survey history. Ask for the last survey and every report since. A boat that has been surveyed before has been checked before, and you can compare. - Service records. Engine, generator, gearbox and stabiliser services, with dates and hours, from the people who did them. Gaps matter more than hours. The hull and deck. Look along the topsides in low light for waves, patches and mismatched gelcoat. Check the swim platform and its hydraulics, the deck fittings, the windows and hatch seals, and whether the teak has lifted. Stains on the saloon headlining or around fittings mean water is getting in. Underwater, if she is out. Props for damage, shafts for wear and play, rudders for movement, anodes for how fast they have been used, and the through-hulls and seacocks for corrosion. If she is in the water, ask for her last haul-out record and when the running gear was last pulled. Engines and gensets. Cold start, no smoke after the first minute, a clean engine bay with no fresh oil or coolant, and no leaking from the raw-water pumps. Look at the hour meters and ask whether they match the service records. Electrics and systems. Shore power, batteries and chargers, air conditioning, the generator under load, thrusters, windlass, pumps, bilge alarms and navigation electronics. Turn everything on at once and listen. Stabilisers. Fins or gyro, whichever she has. Ask when they were last serviced, and test them at the sea trial. Worth knowing A survey is the report. It is not a guarantee. Parts that cannot be reached, such as fuel tanks boxed in behind joinery, are listed as not inspected, and specialist items like complex electronics or carbon fibre may need a specialist. Read the exclusions page as carefully as the findings. Red flags The seller will not allow a survey, a lift-out or a sea trial. Walk away. A “preferred” surveyor. A broker or seller steering you to one person is a reason to choose someone else. Records that stop. Missing service history for the engines, generators or stabilisers. Fresh paint in odd places. In the engine room, around the bilges, below the waterline or on one side only. Hour meters that do not match the logbook. A hull identification number or plate that is missing, altered or does not match the paperwork. Water where water should not be. Damp lockers, soft deck, a smell in the bilge. Pressure. A deposit with no subject-to-survey clause, or a price good only until the show finishes. What a surveyor does A surveyor inspects the hull, structure, systems and safety gear, takes moisture readings, reviews the documents, runs the sea trial and writes a report with photographs. The published Gold Coast rates include the sea trial. In practice you also get a list of defects that you can use to negotiate or to walk away. There is no regulation that sets minimum qualifications for calling yourself a marine surveyor, so the credentials need checking. The Australasian Institute of Marine Surveyors vets its members and assigns membership levels that reflect their experience, and you can search its database. Beyond that, ask whether they carry professional indemnity insurance, whether they have surveyed your make of boat, and for a sample report. Engines are the common gap. Some surveyors do not inspect engines, and others only confirm they run. For big diesels, book an independent marine engineer who knows the make, ideally not the one who last serviced them. Oil analysis and a borescope inspection are the usual tools. What a survey costs in Australia Two Gold Coast and Brisbane firms publish their rates. These are what they say today, with GST included. Boat length Maritime Surveyor BoatBuy 30 to 36 ft $899 $1,075 (30 to 39 ft) 37 to 43 ft $1,099 $1,075 (to 39 ft), $1,300 (40 to 49 ft) 44 to 49 ft $1,299 $1,300 50 to 55 ft $1,499 $1,600 (50 to 59 ft) 56 ft and over Quote on application $1,600 to 59 ft, then quote from 60 ft BoatBuy adds $210 for each engine inspected, $210 per generator, $185 per oil sample and $265 per tender. Maritime Surveyor prices a marine engine oil analysis from $199 and quotes thermography, ultrasonic thickness testing, moisture meter testing and endoscope inspections on application. Maritime Surveyor’s page also lists a lower “special price” that runs to 20 December 2026. Neither page gives a price for the lift-out. That is the yard’s, so ask for a quote. A worked example. A 55 ft twin-engine motor yacht with one generator, on BoatBuy’s published rates: Item Cost Survey, 50 to 59 ft, includes sea trial $1,600 Two engines at $210 $420 One generator $210 Three oil samples at $185 $555 Total before lift-out $2,785 On Maritime Surveyor’s published rates the same boat is $1,499, plus three oil analyses from $199 each, or from $2,096. The lift-out is on top. From 56 or 60 ft, up to the 120 ft end of this audience, the price is on application: ask for it in writing and ask what it includes. {{cta}} When to call a surveyor, and when to call someone else Call a surveyor when you are serious about a boat and the seller has agreed to a survey and sea trial, so the money is spent on a boat that has passed your own inspection. Do not pay for a full survey on a boat that failed your walk-through. Call a specialist on top when the survey leaves a question. A marine engineer for the engines and gensets, a stabiliser technician for the fins or gyro, and an electrician if the electrics are complicated. Each is a few hundred dollars and each can find a five-figure problem. How we help We are a yacht management company, not a surveying firm, so we do not replace the surveyor. What we do is the work around the survey. Marine HQ runs a pre-purchase consultation for buyers. We look at the listing with you before you spend anything, go through the boat with you, read the survey report and the service records against what the boat will need, and put a Gold Coast figure on each finding and on running her here. You then go back to the seller with a list that is priced, not just a list. {{product:pre-purchase-checklist}} After you buy Transfer the registration within 14 days. At 15 m or longer the application must be endorsed by Maritime Safety Queensland before Transport and Main Roads can process it. Insure her from the day you take delivery, and book your first haul-out. Our annual haul-out checklist is the scope to start from, and the size guide covers the running costs you are signing up for.

t: How to get into the yachting industry in Australia: courses, first jobs and who to call
d: The certificates, courses and first jobs that get a new deckhand, stewardess, engineer or chef onto a yacht in Australia, what entry-level crew are paid, and how to get in front of Marine HQ.
x: What the work is The first steps Going further than entry level What a first job pays How people actually get their first boat How to contact Marine HQ Do I need any experience to work on a yacht? What is STCW basic safety training and do I need it? Do I need a medical? How much does an entry-level yacht crew member earn? Do I need to be on the Gold Coast to start? Can I go straight to captain? The usual way into yachting in Australia is short and cheap compared with most careers: a medical, the STCW basic safety course (about eight days), an entry-level deckhand or stewardess course if you want one, and a CV that shows you can turn up on time and work hard. Then you do daywork, get known, and a recruiter or a captain puts you on your first boat. Entry pay is modest, and the career runs from there to captain or chief engineer if you build the sea time. This guide sets out the steps, what they cost in time, what a first job pays and how to get in front of Marine HQ. Key facts - The baseline — STCW basic safety training (about 8 days) and a certificate of medical fitness - Entry roles — deckhand, steward/ess, junior engineer, crew chef - Entry pay — junior deckhand or steward/ess $3,000–$3,500 a month plus super on a 100–120 ft yacht (Crew Pacific, March 2022) - Daywork — $150–$500 a day freelance, depending on experience; $400 a day for a temporary deckhand on a Gold Coast 30 m-plus - Bases — Gold Coast, Sydney and the Whitsundays are the main ones for larger motor yachts - Contact — 0439 748 387 or yachtsupport@marinehq.com.au What the work is Yacht crew are not on holiday, and the best first-timers work that out in the first week. A deckhand washes, polishes, handles lines, drives the tender, and does the maintenance that keeps the boat looking new. A steward or stewardess runs the interior: housekeeping, laundry, service, provisioning. Engineers look after engines, generators and systems. Chefs cook for the owner, guests and crew. Days are long, the weekend is often a working day, and you live in close quarters. In return the food, the uniform and the travel to the vessel are normally provided, and the pay is good for a first job. The first steps Book a medical. A certificate of medical fitness is part of the standard kit. AMSA’s medical rules for seafarers are in Marine Order 76. Do this first; a problem found after paying for courses is expensive. Do the STCW basic safety course. Superyacht Australia’s guide for newcomers calls STCW the mandatory baseline set by the International Maritime Organisation and says it takes about eight days with theory and practical work. Superyacht Crew Academy at Warriewood in Sydney runs the course, with intakes every three weeks, and Crew Pacific in Cairns runs it too. Ask any provider for the full price, including materials. Add a role course if you want one. Deckhand and stewardess courses are offered by the same providers. For deck, a powerboat licence and tender driving help; for interior, hospitality, silver service and mixology; for the galley, a cookery qualification. Write the CV. One page, a recent photo, your certificates and expiry dates, and anything useful: cooking, childcare, drone work, photography, trades. Denison Yachting’s guide for new crew puts it bluntly: you must have a great CV, and a portfolio helps (before-and-after deck work for deckhands, food and table settings for stews and chefs). Get in front of recruiters and captains. Australian recruiters place “green” crew in their first role. The Superyacht Australia guide names Hill Maritime and Coastal Yachting Recruitment on the Gold Coast, and boards like MYS Superyacht Crew list Australian jobs. You can also contact us. Going further than entry level If you plan to stay, the next step is a commercial ticket, and AMSA runs the national system. General Purpose Hand and Coxswain. Entry-level domestic commercial tickets, available through AMSA-approved training providers; Superyacht Crew Academy lists General Purpose Hand, Coxswain and Master less than 24 m among its AMSA courses. TAFE Queensland’s Coomera campus runs Coxswain Grade 1 as a four-week course ($4,645 full fee, $1,665 subsidised, as quoted in our guide on full-time crew). Master less than 24 metres. AMSA’s certificate for the master of a vessel under 24 m; since January 2023 it replaced the old Mate under 80 m certificate. Sea time and an assessment are required. Engineering. Crew Pacific’s pay guide lists chief and second engineers by Marine Engine Driver (MED) grade, so check AMSA’s engineering certificates and ask an approved training provider where to start. Overseas tickets. Some people arrive with UK or international yacht certificates. AMSA’s rules on recognising them are separate and change, so check with AMSA before you pay for anything. What a first job pays Published pay is thin, so here is what there is, with dates. Role What was published Junior deckhand, 100–120 ft $3,000–$3,500 a month plus super (Crew Pacific, March 2022) Junior steward/ess, 100–120 ft $3,000–$3,500 a month plus super (Crew Pacific, March 2022) Freelance deckhand, mate or steward/ess $150–$500 a day depending on experience (Crew Pacific) Temporary deckhand, 30 m-plus private yacht, Gold Coast $400 a day (listing on MYS) Yachts commonly pay for food, uniforms and travel to the boat, and health insurance after a 30 to 90-day trial. Four weeks’ paid holiday and a five-and-a-half or six-day week are described as normal. Private yachts generally pay a higher base than charter yachts because there are no charter tips. {{product:crew-starter-kit}} How people actually get their first boat Daywork is how most people start. A captain or head of department tries you for a few days, and if you are good, somebody remembers. Denison’s guide says the same: temporary work can lead to a full-time role. Turn up early, do the unglamorous job properly, and ask what to do next. After that: Be reachable. Answer the phone and reply quickly; a captain with a gap will not wait long. Keep certificates current. Check expiry dates; STCW refresher courses are a cost, and expired certificates cost you the job. Stay in touch with agents. If you are still looking, tell them, so they remember you. Be where the boats are. The Gold Coast, Sydney and the Whitsundays are the main bases; most employers prefer candidates already in Australia. {{cta}} How to contact Marine HQ Marine HQ places crew on motor yachts across Australia and looks after yachts day to day from The Boat Works and Gold Coast City Marina & Shipyard in Coomera. We hear from yacht owners who need crew, and from people who want to work on a yacht, and we like to talk to both. To get in front of us, send: your CV with a recent photo copies of your certificates and medical, with expiry dates the roles you want (deck, interior, engineering, galley) and any experience where you are based and the dates you are free two references, if you have them The quickest way is to join our crew register on the crew placement page , which takes about five minutes. You can also email yachtsupport@marinehq.com.au or call 0439 748 387. We cannot promise a job, but we will read what you send and tell you plainly where you stand. If you are an owner looking for crew instead, see how to hire yacht crew in Australia .

t: How to hire yacht crew in Australia: roles, pay, agency fees and the paperwork
d: Who to hire for a 40–120 ft motor yacht in Australia, what captains, engineers, deckhands and stewardesses are paid, what crew agencies charge, and the checks to make before anyone steps aboard.
x: Who you actually need What crew are paid The real cost of a full-time hire What a crewing agency does for its fee Doing it yourself The paperwork References and the first month Marine HQ crew placement If you are looking for yacht work How much does a crew agency charge to place a captain or deckhand? What is a replacement guarantee? Can I just advertise and hire crew myself? What qualifications does a captain need? What does day crew cost? Do I need a Queensland labour hire licence to supply crew, or to use a crew supplier? Can I hire a foreign crew member? Hiring yacht crew in Australia is a people decision with a paperwork tail. The usual routes are an agency, which typically charges roughly 8% to 10% of a year’s salary for a permanent placement; a job board and your own screening; or a management company that does it for you. Pay runs from about $150 to $500 a day for freelance crew, to $10,000 to $14,000 a month for a captain on a 100 to 120 ft yacht, including super. This guide sets out who you actually need, what they cost, what an agency does for its fee, and the checks to make before anyone steps aboard. Key facts - Agency fee, permanent — 8% to 10% of annual salary, or 75% to 100% of a month’s pay, depending on the agency - Agency fee, temporary — 25% to 30% of daily pay; seasonal (30 to 180 days) 70% to 80% of a month - Guarantee — 60 days is the shortest in one industry guide; many match the 90-day probation - Freelance day rates — captain $350–$500, engineer $300–$500, deckhand or mate $150–$500, steward/ess $150–$500 - Captain, 100–120 ft — $10,000 to $14,000 a month including super (Crew Pacific, March 2022) - Employer on-costs — 12% super and WorkCover on top of salary; four weeks’ paid leave is the industry norm Who you actually need The first question is not who, but how many. On a boat of 40 to 60 ft used on weekends, the answer is often nobody full time: an owner at the helm and a day deckhand or a maintenance crew for the washing, checking and turnarounds. Our guide on full-time crew walks through the four ways to run a yacht and what each costs. If you have decided that someone will be aboard, here are the roles. Role What they do When you need one Captain Runs the boat, the crew, the budget and the compliance Most yachts above about 65 to 75 ft that are used regularly Engineer Engines, generators, systems, the engine room log Larger yachts and any yacht on a long-range programme; below that, a captain with technical skills and a trades network Mate / first officer Second in command, deck, tender, watchkeeping on passages Yachts that cruise, and any passage with a night leg Deckhand / bosun Washing, polishing, lines, tender, deck maintenance The day-to-day upkeep: the “other forty hours a week” Steward / stewardess, chief stew Interior, guests, provisioning, laundry, service Yachts that host, charter or have owners aboard for long stays Chef Galley, menus and provisioning Yachts with a lot of guests and extended cruises A crew of two, captain and deckhand or captain and stewardess, is how many private yachts around 60 to 80 ft are run. Add a third person at the point where somebody is always on duty or the boat is used for guests. What crew are paid There is no single Australian pay survey for yacht crew, so any number needs a date and a source. These are the published ones. Full-time, large yachts. The Crew Pacific salary guidelines (March 2022, Australian dollars per month, superannuation to be included on top) start at the 100 to 120 ft band: Role 100–120 ft 120–140 ft Captain $10,000–$14,000 $14,000–$16,000 Chief engineer (MED 1–3) $8,000–$9,000 $9,000–$10,000 First mate / first officer $6,000–$7,000 $7,000–$8,000 Second mate (OOW) $5,000–$6,000 $6,000–$7,000 Bosun $3,500–$4,000 $5,000–$6,000 Deckhand with experience $3,000–$3,500 $3,500–$3,800 Chef $5,500–$6,500 $6,500–$8,000 Chief steward/ess $4,500–$5,000 $6,000–$7,000 Steward/ess with experience $3,200–$3,500 $3,500–$4,000 Freelance and delivery work (per day, Crew Pacific). Captain $350–$500; engineer $300–$500; deckhand or mate $150–$500; chef $200–$500; steward/ess $150–$500, “pending experience”. The guide also says it is standard for the yacht to provide return fares to the vessel, food, uniforms and transport, that health insurance is usually provided after a 30 to 90-day evaluation period, that four weeks’ paid holiday is normal, and that private yachts generally pay a higher base because there are no charter tips. Smaller boats, live examples. Published pay for a 40 to 80 ft private yacht is scarce. A Gold Coast listing (Queensland) for a temporary deckhand on a 30 m-plus private motor yacht was $400 a day. A year-round Gold Coast (Queensland) interior manager role for a yacht-share company, advertised on 12 May 2023, was $68,000 plus super, about 40 hours a week and four weeks’ paid leave. The listing has expired; treat it as a dated example, not a current rate. The 2022 table is four years old. Check it against what your own market is telling you; pay varies by port and by season. The real cost of a full-time hire Take a captain on a $100,000 base. Add 12% superannuation and about 1.3% WorkCover, and the employer cost is about $113,000 before leave, flights, training and the relief cover for four weeks’ holiday. Put an agency on top at 8% to 10% for the first year and the first-year cost is $8,000 to $10,000 more, once. That is the arithmetic; the agency’s real quote will depend on its own terms. Replacement costs more than recruitment. Industry turnover runs at 20% to 40% a year, and the price of a poor hire is a season of stalled maintenance. That is why the fee is worth less than the process around it, as the next two sections explain. {{cta}} What a crewing agency does for its fee A good agency is not a job board. For the fee it should: Know the candidate. Check qualifications and references before it sends a CV, and place only people it would put on its own boat. Understand the boat. The owner’s habits, the family, the existing crew, the itinerary and whether the yacht charters. A captain who suits a quiet private yacht may be wrong for a charter programme. Check the paperwork. Certificates, medicals, the right to work, and a written employment agreement before a start date. Stand behind the placement. A replacement guarantee, a follow-up call a few weeks in, and someone to ring when it is not working. The fee models published by one industry guide are worth knowing. Permanent placement is 8% to 10% of annual salary, or 75% to 100% of a monthly salary. Seasonal crew (30 to 180 days) are 70% to 80% of a gross month, and temporary placements of 1 to 29 days are 25% to 30% of gross daily pay. Some agencies discount repeat clients, 10% off a second placement and 20% off a third, and some offer a monthly retainer that covers all crew. The shortest guarantee in that guide was 60 days, with many agencies matching the 90-day probation. A worked example. Captain on $100,000: permanent fee of 8% to 10% is $8,000 to $10,000; at 75% to 100% of one month ($8,333) it is $6,250 to $8,333. A ten-day relief deckhand at $400 a day earns $4,000, and a 25% temporary fee is $1,000. The yacht normally pays; under the Maritime Labour Convention practice, a crew member is not charged to be placed. Before you sign Ask for the fee schedule, the guarantee period and what happens if the candidate leaves in week ten, in writing. “We will look after you” is not a guarantee. {{product:crew-hiring-pack}} Doing it yourself You can hire without an agency. Then the work is yours: screen CVs, interview, call at least two previous captains or owners, prepare the employment agreement, run payroll and superannuation, arrange leave and insurance, and arrange a trial period. The trap is the first month. A new captain who arrives to find no maintenance schedule, no vendor list and no history will spend three weeks learning the boat from scratch, and an unhappy first month is how a placement fails. If you manage the boat through a management company, the manager usually handles the hiring, the handover and the paperwork, and the boat’s record stays put when crew change. The paperwork Qualifications. Rules depend on how the yacht is used. A yacht used only for recreation is not a domestic commercial vessel, even though paid crew run her, and AMSA says paying someone to crew her does not change that. If she is chartered or hired out, she is a domestic commercial vessel and her master needs the right certificate of competency; for most yachts under 24 m that is a Master less than 24 metres certificate under Marine Order 505, which replaced the old Mate under 80 m certificate in January 2023. Even on a private yacht, a captain with the certificate has had their sea time tested. Medical fitness. AMSA requires a certificate of medical fitness for seafarers who apply for a certificate of competency; the rules sit in Marine Order 76. Ask to see the certificate. Training. Ask for current first aid, sea survival and firefighting training, and for the engineer, the engine tickets that match the engines. Don’t assume; read the certificate and note the expiry date. Employment basics. Superannuation at 12%, WorkCover, a written agreement, rest time, paid leave and a probation period. Industry guidance is at least 10 hours’ rest in any 24 and four weeks’ paid leave a year. Get advice on which agreement or award applies to your boat; we could not find a published answer for private-yacht crew. Visas. Foreign crew need permission to work in Australia. The Maritime Crew visa is aimed at commercial ships and the Home Affairs form says crew of yachts do not normally qualify, so ask a registered migration agent before you make an offer. Labour hire. Queensland requires a labour hire licence (other states have their own rules, so check where the yacht is based) for anyone who supplies workers to work for another business, and it is an offence to use a provider that does not hold one. A recruiter introducing someone you employ is a different thing; a firm sending you its own staff by the day is labour hire. Ask for the licence number and check the register. References and the first month References first, on the phone. Call the last two captains or owners, and ask three things: would you employ them again, how did they handle a bad day, and why did they leave. A written reference tells you nothing a phone call will not. The first month is the probation. Agree it in writing, set a handover list (open defects, logs, contacts, safety gear, passwords) and walk the boat together. A good handover is a week of overlap with the last captain; if that is not possible, have a handover record that stays with the boat. See full-time crew for what leaves when a captain does. Marine HQ crew placement Marine HQ places crew on motor yachts across Australia: captains, engineers, mates, deckhands, stewards and stewardesses, for permanent roles, seasons, deliveries and short relief cover. We are a yacht management company first, so we place people who will be working on boats like yours, and we know what a good handover looks like. You tell us the boat and the job. Size, programme, home port, how often she is used, whether she charters and who is already aboard. We find and check the people. Certificates, medical, sea time and references, before a CV reaches you. We shortlist and introduce. You meet the people we would put on the boat ourselves. We help with the start. A written agreement, a handover list and a check-in once they are aboard. For work on the water in between, our team covers relief and delivery skipping, wash-downs, day work and maintenance, from our bases at The Boat Works and Gold Coast City Marina & Shipyard in Coomera, Queensland. Tell us the role, the boat and the dates on our crew placement page , or call 0439 748 387 or email yachtsupport@marinehq.com.au, and we will tell you how we can help and what it will cost. If you are looking for yacht work If you are a captain, engineer, deckhand or stewardess looking for work anywhere in Australia, see how to get into the yachting industry and send us your CV, your certificates, your sea time and the dates you are available. We cannot promise a job, but we will talk to you. The best things you can have ready are current certificates and medical, two references from previous yachts, and a clear idea of the kind of boat and programme you want.

t: Antifouling on the Gold Coast: what it costs and what's actually in the job
d: Per-foot yard packages, hardstand rates, paint prices, Propspeed and anodes, how often to do it in Gold Coast water, and a worked example for a 60 ft motor yacht.
x: The short answer What is actually in the job What the Gold Coast yards publish The extras, line by line Paint: what it costs and how much you need How often, and what fouling costs you The rules Timing Worked example: 60 ft twin-shaft motor yacht What to check before you sign What we do How much does antifouling cost on the Gold Coast? How often should I antifoul on the Gold Coast? Can I clean the hull in the water instead? What does Propspeed cost? How long is she out of the water? Which antifoul paint should I use? For a fibreglass motor yacht up to 50 ft , the clearest number on the Gold Coast is Gold Coast City Marina’s package: from $89.50 a foot , haul-out to relaunch, about $4,475 for a 50-footer. Above 50 ft, every yard quotes. Build it from the published parts and a 60 ft motor yacht lands around $6,700 for antifoul, Propspeed and anodes, and closer to $9,000 once you add the hull polish most owners want while she is out. Here is what is in the job, what each line costs, and what to check before you sign. Key facts — Gold Coast, 2026 - Package, to 50 ft — from $89.50/ft at GCCM, including haul, waterblast, levy, four days’ hardstand, paint and application - Applicator only — Harbourforce from $51/ft standard, $86/ft with hull cut and polish, $240/ft blast and re-antifoul - Hardstand — The Boat Works has quoted from $2.20 a foot a night; GCCM’s undercover bay is $1 a foot a day extra - Paint — 20 litres for a 60-footer by roller; $1,700 for two 10 L tins of Micron Extra 2 - How often — 12 months locally, 12 to 18 months per the insurers - Lead time — book four to six weeks ahead; longer before summer and the May boat show The short answer $89.50/ft GCCM package, fibreglass monohulls to 50 ft ~$6,700 60 ft: antifoul + Propspeed + anodes, built from published rates 3–5 days on the hardstand, paint plus extras +20–25% fuel burn from slime on half the hull (IMO study) The per-foot number is real, but it describes the paint job. On a 60 ft motor yacht the running gear, the anodes, the seacocks and the polish are where the rest of the bill and most of the value sit. What is actually in the job Haul-out. Travelift from the water to the hardstand. The Coomera yards run 300-tonne lifts; Runaway Bay's stops at 16 m. Waterblast and environmental levy. High-pressure wash on a wash-down pad that captures the run-off. The levy is the yard's cost of doing that legally. Inspection. Hull, existing paint, anodes, skin fittings, props, shafts, rudders and seals. This is the moment to find the problem, not after relaunch. Preparation. Wet sand, never dry sand or burn off; mask the waterline; prime any bare patches. Paint. Two full coats, a third on the waterline, chines, rudders and leading edges. Running gear. Propspeed on props, shafts and rudders; new anodes; prop polish if wanted. Extras while she is out. Hull cut and polish, seacock service, skeg bearings, moisture checks. Relaunch. Micron One has to be back in the water within one to three months; Micron Extra 2 will wait up to 12. What the Gold Coast yards publish Very little, which is why the same haul-out gets quoted three different ways. Provider What is published Notes Gold Coast City Marina & Shipyard Package from $89.50/ft Fibreglass monohulls to 50 ft only, antifouled within two years, subject to inspection. Includes haul and relaunch, waterblast, levy, four days’ hardstand, International Micron One or similar, running-gear check, project management. Over 50 ft: personalised quote. GCCM undercover bay $1/ft/day on top of hardstand Covered bays to 100 ft with 18 m air draught. Harbourforce Marine (GCCM and The Boat Works) Standard antifoul from $51/ft; antifoul and detailing from $86/ft; sandblast and antifoul from $240/ft Two coats, three on leading edges, washdown. Excludes lift, hardstand, Propspeed and additional work. The Boat Works No prices; hardstand quoted from $2.20/ft/night up to 20 ft beam, $2.30 wider Six to fifteen months between antifouls “a good rule of thumb”. Book four to six weeks ahead. Short Marine, Gold Coast Antifouling, ADG Marine, Pronto, Antifoul Solutions Quote only Short Marine says it does the job over 1,000 times a year; Runaway Bay lifts to 16 m. GCCM’s package tells the story of the market: $69 a foot when it launched around 2020, $85 a foot on older pages still live today, $89.50 now. Roughly 30% in five or six years. The extras, line by line Propspeed. A silicone foul-release coating on the props, shafts and rudders. Reported Australian shipwright quotes sit around $850 for a twin-prop set once the labour is honest, with cheaper quotes of $450 that the trade says undercharge; the New Zealand benchmark for a twin-prop 13 m boat is NZ$1,200. Two 500 ml kits are about $478 in materials alone. Lasts a year at minimum and up to three. Watson Marine at Coomera is the approved applicator and also scans, repitches and polishes props. Anodes. Shaft collars are $25 to $65 each, hull blocks about $38, so $250 to $400 in parts for a twin-shaft boat with a few hull anodes. Fitting labour is not published anywhere and is usually bundled. Hull cut and polish. Harbourforce’s two package prices imply $35 a foot for a waterline-to-gunwale cut and polish, so $2,100 on a 60-footer. Doing it on the hardstand is cheaper and better than doing it in the water. Seacocks, skin fittings, skeg bearings. Offered as quote items by the shipwrights. Not published. Have them exercised and inspected every haul-out regardless. Moisture and blister checks. No Australian pricing published. Ask; on an older hull it is worth more than the paint. Before you sign A “from $X a foot” quote is a paint quote. Ask in writing whether it includes the lift both ways, the waterblast and levy, the number of hardstand days, the paint grade and litres, Propspeed, anodes and the polish. If it does not say, it is not included. Paint: what it costs and how much you need Paint Type Coverage by roller 10 L tin, inc GST International Micron One Ablative copper; GCCM’s standard 5.4 m²/L, 2 coats $582 International Micron Extra 2 Polishing copolymer, two seasons from one application 9 m²/L, 3 coats by brush or 2 by spray plus stripe coat $848 International Micron AP Boosted biocide for high-fouling tropical water 4 m²/L $469 per 4 L Jotun SeaVictor 40 Entry-level single-pack, black only $407 ex GST Jotun SeaForce Active Self-polishing, commercial grade $320 to $360 per 5 L International Trilux 33 Copper-free for aluminium hulls, up to 18 months 9 m²/L, 3 coats from $154 per 750 mL How much: wetted area is roughly length times beam times 0.85. A Sunseeker Manhattan 60 at 19.60 m by 5.0 m is about 83 m². With Micron Extra 2 by roller at 9 m² a litre, two coats and a stripe coat is about 20 litres, two 10 L tins, $1,696 . By spray the coverage halves and the litres double. With Micron One at 5.4 m² a litre it is about 31 litres, so three to four 10 L tins, about $1,750 to $2,330. Spraying costs more paint, not less; it buys a better finish. Hard or soft? Ablative or self-polishing paints wear away as the boat moves and suit boats that are used. Hard antifouls need scrubbing and suit boats that sit. For a motor yacht that goes out, ablative. For an aluminium hull, copper-free, always. How often, and what fouling costs you The local applicators say once a year in Gold Coast water. Nautilus, the insurer, says every 12 to 18 months regardless of size. The Boat Works says six to fifteen months. Brisbane yards put frequently used powerboats at six to twelve months and only dry-stored boats at 18 to 24. The national biofouling guidelines add that coatings should be renewed towards the shorter end of their rated life, and that you should keep the paint invoices and slipway receipts. The reason to keep to it is fuel. An IMO study found slime as thin as half a millimetre over half the hull adds 20% to 25% to fuel burn, and a light layer of barnacles up to 55%. A 2025 KTH study measured slime alone raising the power needed by up to 18%. Those are ship figures, but the physics is the same on a 60 ft Sunseeker burning 196 litres an hour at 20 knots. A season on a fouled hull can cost more in diesel than the antifoul did. The rules In-water hull scraping is generally not allowed in Australia without permission, and Queensland’s guidance is to do the work in a yard or slipway with a compliant wash-down system. If you want an in-water clean you ask Biosecurity Queensland, the environment department or Maritime Safety Queensland first, depending on where the boat is. Tributyltin paints have been banned on vessels under 25 m since 1989. None of this is new, but it is why the yard charges an environmental levy and why the diver with a scraper is not a shortcut. {{cta}} Timing Days out. Modern coatings overcoat in six hours and can be launched eight hours after the final coat at 23 °C, so the paint is a two-day job. Propspeed, anodes and drying make it three to five. Bundle an engine service or the annual list and GCCM’s guide says one to two weeks. Lead time. The Boat Works asks for four to six weeks’ notice. Demand jumps as the warm months approach, and the yards run hardstand specials through winter for exactly that reason. The boat show. Sanctuary Cove International Boat Show runs 20 to 23 May 2027. Yards and trades are flat out in the weeks before it. Launch window. Micron One must be immersed within one to three months of painting. If other work will keep her on the hard, paint last, or use Micron Extra 2, which tolerates 12 months out. Worked example: 60 ft twin-shaft motor yacht Every line is from a published rate above or marked as a quote item. Line Route A: GCCM package extrapolated Route B: The Boat Works plus applicator Antifoul incl. lift, waterblast, levy, 4 days’ hardstand, standard paint $5,370 (60 ft at $89.50/ft; package caps at 50 ft, so treat as a floor) Applicator $3,060 (60 ft at $51/ft) plus hardstand $528 (4 nights at $2.20/ft) plus lift, wash and levy: quote Propspeed, props, shafts, rudders $850 to $1,200 $850 to $1,200 Anodes, parts $250 to $400 $250 to $400 Antifoul, Propspeed, anodes about $6,700 about $5,000 plus lift fees Hull cut and polish $2,100 (60 ft at $35/ft) $2,100 With polish about $8,800 about $7,100 plus lift fees Upgrading from Micron One to Micron Extra 2 changes the tin cost by almost nothing at roller rates and buys a two-season claim. Seacocks, bearings, moisture work and any gelcoat repairs are on top. That is why the $10,000 allowance in our cost-of-ownership guide is a fair working number for a 60-footer, and why a neglected boat can double it. {{product:haul-out}} What to check before you sign The lift is included both ways, and the number of hardstand days is written down. The paint brand, grade and litres are named. “Or similar” is not a grade. Propspeed, anodes and the polish are separate lines with prices, not “as required”. Someone is inspecting seacocks, shaft seals and skin fittings, and photographing what they find. The relaunch date is booked, not “when it’s done”. What we do Marine HQ scopes the yard visit before the boat comes out, gets the lift, paint, running gear and extras quoted as separate lines, books the slot early enough to avoid the summer queue, and has someone on the hardstand while the work is done. Every stage is photographed into the owner’s MyYacht app, and the antifoul date, paint and litres go into her maintenance record so the next one is booked before it is overdue. If she is due, call 0439 748 387 or email yachtsupport@marinehq.com.au and we will put a number on it.

t: How much does it cost to own a yacht on the Gold Coast? (2026)
d: Berth, antifoul, insurance, servicing, fuel and rego for a 40–120 ft motor yacht on the Gold Coast, with published 2026 figures and a worked example for a 60-footer.
x: The short answer Berthing: the one bill everyone knows about The yard: antifouling and everything that goes with it Insurance Servicing the machinery Registration Fuel: the cost of actually using her Keeping her clean A worked example: 60 ft, about $1.2 million Where the money hides What we do about it Is it cheaper to keep a boat on the Gold Coast than in Sydney? How much is a berth at Sanctuary Cove? Should I buy a marina berth instead of renting? Do I need to antifoul every year on the Gold Coast? What does the 10% rule mean for a yacht? Is registration expensive in Queensland? A 60 ft motor yacht kept on the Gold Coast costs roughly $70,000 to $80,000 a year sitting at the dock , and $130,000 or more once you use her for a hundred hours. Bigger boats, Sanctuary Cove berthing, agreed-value insurance or a big engine year push that higher. Here is where the money goes, using published 2026 rates wherever one exists. Key facts — 60 ft motor yacht, Gold Coast, 2026 - Berth — $1,650 to $2,100 a month at the published rates; more at the resort marinas - Antifoul — every 12 to 18 months; the yard visit is the biggest single maintenance bill - Insurance — 1% to 3% of insured value a year, so $12,000 to $36,000 on a $1.2 million boat - Servicing — engines and generator every year, on hours or calendar, whichever comes first - Registration — $779.05 a year for a 15 to 20 m vessel (from 1 July 2026) - Fuel — about $635 an hour at 20 knots, at $3.24 a litre The short answer $70–80k a year at the dock, 60 ft, worked example below ~$635/hr fuel at 20 knots, 60 ft Sunseeker, $3.24/L 10–15% of vessel value a year, the old rule of thumb 12–18 mo between antifouls in warm Gold Coast water Most owners find the fixed costs are predictable and the variable ones are not. The berth, the insurance and the rego arrive on schedule. The yard visit, the engine service that turns into an injector job, and the fuel bill after a good month on the water are what move the total. Berthing: the one bill everyone knows about Only one Gold Coast marina publishes a full rate card: Southport Yacht Club, effective 1 May 2026. Gold Coast City Marina & Shipyard’s last public schedule is from November 2022 and says rates are subject to change. Sanctuary Cove, Marina Mirage, Hope Harbour, Runaway Bay and The Boat Works all quote on enquiry. Berth Southport YC, Gold Member, per month Southport YC, visitor, per month GCCM, 2022 schedule, per month 40 ft / 12 m double $1,039 $1,745 $1,375 (41–50 ft) 49 ft / 15 m double $1,186 $1,930 $1,375 59 ft / 18 m double $1,797 $2,615 $1,650 (51–60 ft) 59 ft / 18 m single $2,064 $3,145 $1,650 66 ft / 20 m single $2,598 $3,380 $1,925 (61–70 ft) 73 ft / 22 m single $3,174 $4,013 $2,400 (71–80 ft) 82 ft / 25 m single $4,122 $5,500 $3,200 (81–90 ft) A few things the rate card does not shout about: Membership matters at Southport. The visitor rate is 40% to 50% above the Gold Member rate. A 12-month contract on a 59 ft single berth is $19,311 for members. Power is extra. Southport bills three-phase electricity at 35 cents a kilowatt hour. GCCM lists utilities as extra too. Wide and catamaran berths cost 30% to 40% more at Southport; GCCM charges multihulls 1.5 times on a T-head and double in a berth. Rates are climbing. Southport’s 59 ft double berth went from $14,139 a year in May 2023 to $16,087 in May 2026, up 13.8% in three years. New marinas open at the top of the market. Mantaray Marina at The Spit, opened May 2026, advertises monthly leases from $2,000 and twenty superyacht berths. Above 82 ft the rate card stops. Southport quotes berths over 25 m on application. GCCM’s 2022 schedule had 91–100 ft at $5,000 a month and 101–110 ft at $6,000, with vessels over 111 ft at $2.30 a foot a day, about $8,300 a month for a 120-footer. Buying is an option. Freehold berths at Hope Island, next to Sanctuary Cove, list at about $179,000 for 12 m and $320,000 for 18 m, with outgoings of $6,600 to $7,900 a year. Rentals in the same area run $1,050 to $1,300 a month. The yard: antifouling and everything that goes with it Warm water fouls hulls fast, and the Gold Coast is named in industry guides as a high-fouling area. Plan on antifouling every 12 to 18 months, or every 12 to 15 months for an aluminium hull. GCCM’s all-inclusive antifoul package is the clearest published price on the Coast: from $89.50 a foot , including haul-out and relaunch, waterblast, environmental levy, four days on the hardstand, International Micron One or similar, a running-gear check and yard management. It applies to fibreglass monohulls up to 50 ft that were antifouled within the last two years. A 50-footer is therefore about $4,475. Anything larger is a personalised quote. The same package was $69 a foot when it launched in 2020, so it has risen about 30% in six years. For the antifoul work alone, HF Marine Services at GCCM publishes from $51 a foot for a standard two-coat job and from $86 a foot with a hull cut and polish, excluding the yard’s lift and hardstand, Propspeed, anodes and any fairing. Before you sign The per-foot price is never the whole bill. Propspeed on the running gear, new anodes, seacock servicing, a prop polish and any moisture or blister work are quoted separately, and on a 60-footer they add up quickly. Ask for the full scope in writing before she comes out of the water. Our antifouling guide walks through each line. Insurance No Australian insurer publishes a rate as a percentage of hull value. The nearest independent figure is that boat insurance in Australia typically costs 1% to 3% of the insured value a year . On a $1.2 million motor yacht that is $12,000 to $36,000. Where you sit in that range depends on the boat’s age, your experience and claims history, where she is kept and whether you insure for agreed or market value. Queensland has one extra variable: cyclones. Brisbane, the Gold Coast and the Sunshine Coast attract smaller cyclone loadings than the Whitsundays or Cairns, but most policies still require you to haul out or secure the vessel within a set time once a named cyclone is within a defined distance. Nautilus, for example, applies a named-cyclone excess of $5,000 or 5% of the claim, whichever is greater. Read that clause before you buy, not after. Servicing the machinery Engine makers set service intervals on hours or calendar time, whichever comes first . For most leisure boats that means an annual service whether you did 40 hours or 400. Volvo Penta’s D-series has a 250-hour or yearly service (filters, belts, seawater pump, anodes) and a 500-hour or two-yearly service on top; IPS pods add gear oil, drive anodes and diagnostics, and a five-yearly pod service out of the water. Generators run on a similar pattern, with oil at 150 hours or yearly on an Onan and an annual impeller, filter and anode change on a Kohler. Australian guides put a routine inboard engine service at $1,000 to $5,000 per engine , and unplanned repairs at a further $1,000 to $5,000 a year. Those figures skew small; a twin-engine 60-footer with a generator should allow for the upper end every year and for a much larger bill in a 1,000-hour year, when injectors, aftercoolers and heat exchangers come due. No Australian dealer publishes fixed prices for a Volvo IPS, MAN, MTU or Caterpillar major, so get it quoted early. Seatech Marine at The Boat Works is the authorised Kohler, Onan and Caterpillar dealer on the Coast. Registration Queensland registration is one of the cheaper lines. The fee is set in the Transport Operations (Marine Safety) Regulation and indexed each July. Vessel length 2025–26 From 1 July 2026 Over 10 m to 15 m (33 to 49 ft) $608.05 $628.60 Over 15 m to 20 m (49 to 66 ft) $753.60 $779.05 Over 20 m (66 ft and up) $948.25 $980.25 Vessels of 15 m and over have one extra step: any new registration, transfer or change of particulars must be endorsed by Maritime Safety Queensland before a Transport and Main Roads service centre will process it. {{cta}} Fuel: the cost of actually using her Marina diesel in south-east Queensland was $3.19 to $3.24 a litre at the Royal Queensland Yacht Squadron on 1 October 2026, the nearest published pump price to the Gold Coast. That is about 14% more than the $2.79 to $2.84 the same club listed on 3 September. Southport Yacht Club gives Gold Members 6 cents a litre off at its 24-hour fuel wharf, and Sanctuary Cove offers bulk pricing on fills over 1,000 litres. Date any figure you rely on. What a luxury motor yacht burns, from published sea trials: Yacht Engines Speed Burn Cost an hour at $3.24 Sunseeker Manhattan 60 (64 ft) Twin MAN V8-900, 900 hp 20.0 knots 196 L/h $635 23.6 knots 256 L/h $829 Azimut S7 (71 ft) Three Volvo Penta D13 IPS1050 24.8 knots 245 L/h $794 28.9 knots 326 L/h $1,056 Pershing GTX80 Three Volvo Penta D13 IPS1350 10 knots 68 L/h $221 28 knots 439 L/h $1,423 At 196 litres an hour and $3.24 a litre, a 60 ft Sunseeker costs about $635 an hour underway at its best cruise of 20 knots, and $829 an hour at 23.6 knots. A hundred hours at 20 knots is $63,504, and the generator, running at anchor and overnight, is on top. Speed moves the bill more than anything else: the Pershing costs $221 an hour at 10 knots and $1,423 at 28. Our guide to yacht fuel cost sets out the burn, cost per mile and a full-tank price for each boat. Keeping her clean Every Gold Coast detailer quotes on request; none publishes a price list. The nearest published Australian rates are a Sydney yard’s: a wash at $4.75 to $5.00 a foot for 41 to 60 ft boats, wax from $3 a foot and a cut and polish at $18 to $20 a foot. On that basis a 60-footer is about $300 a wash and roughly $7,800 a year fortnightly . A full cut and polish is a four-figure job and usually timed with the yard visit. Move her to a resort marina, insure at the top of the range or hit a 1,000-hour service and you are past $150,000 without trying. It is also why the 10% rule tends to hold: on a new $2.2 million yacht of this size, 10% is $220,000, and a well-used boat of that size can spend it. {{product:calculator}} Where the money hides The gap between “at the dock” and “in use” is fuel. Decide how much you will really use her before you decide what she costs. The yard year. Antifoul is annual-ish, but a pod service, a shaft seal or an aftercooler can double the bill in the year it falls due. Member versus visitor. At Southport the difference on a 59 ft single berth is about $13,000 a year. Cyclone clauses. Cheaper cover with a haul-out requirement is not cheaper if the yard has no space when a cyclone is named. Everything is quote-only above 50 ft. The only way to know is to ask, and to ask for the full scope. What we do about it Marine HQ runs the maintenance for motor yachts across the Gold Coast, and the budget is part of that.
