t: Taking your motor yacht from the Gold Coast to Sydney
d: About 470 nautical miles, three to six days. The legs, the all-weather harbours and the bar entrances, the East Australian Current, fuel and berths in Sydney, the NSW rules, and whether to run her yourself or send a delivery skipper.
x: The legs Harbours: all-weather or bar Weather and the current Fuel Where to berth in Sydney The NSW rules that catch Queensland boats Run her yourself, or send her down What we do How far is it from the Gold Coast to Sydney by sea? How long does the trip take in a motor yacht? Which harbours can I enter in any weather? What is the East Australian Current and does it help? Do I need NSW registration or a NSW licence? What does a delivery skipper cost? Gold Coast to Sydney is about 470 nautical miles of open coast, with the East Australian Current behind you and a handful of genuinely all-weather harbours to break it up. A 20-knot motor yacht does it in three or four days with the weather on side; a displacement boat in five to seven. The coast is not difficult, but it punishes impatience: most of the trouble on this run comes from crossing a bar on the wrong tide or leaving port into a southerly change. Here is how to plan it, and what to do when you get there. Key facts - Distance — about 470 nm Seaway to Sydney Heads; plot your own legs before trusting any table - Time — 21 to 26 hours’ running at 18 to 22 knots; three to four days with stops; five to seven at displacement speed - All-weather harbours — Sydney, Newcastle, Port Stephens; Coffs Harbour has no bar but a shoaling entrance - Bar entrances — Ballina, Yamba, Port Macquarie, Camden Haven, Forster, Swansea: lifejackets on, incoming tide only - Current — the East Australian Current sets south at 2 to 3 knots, sometimes nearly 4; it is your friend this way - Season — spring onwards, when the northerlies arrive; East Coast Lows peak June and July The legs The track at a glance, Seaway to Sydney Harbour. {{map:gold-coast-to-sydney}} The distances below are drawn from sail-training and cruising sources and do not agree with each other to the mile. Use them for planning, then measure the legs on your own chart with the offshore distance you actually intend to run. Leg Distance Notes Gold Coast Seaway to Yamba (Clarence River) overnight run; 12 to 16 hours in a slow boat Cross the Seaway on the flood; arrive Yamba one to two hours before high water Yamba to Coffs Harbour about 58 nm Coffs has no bar; the 2025 rebuild gave it 143 new berths for 10 to 30 m Coffs Harbour to Port Macquarie about 72 nm Port Macquarie is a designated bar; Marine Rescue there has a bar webcam Port Macquarie to Camden Haven (Laurieton) about 20 nm Bar entrance Camden Haven to Port Stephens about 83 nm, via Forster if needed Forster is one of the better bars, protected from southerlies by Cape Hawke Port Stephens to Newcastle about 26 nm Both deep, wide, no bar Newcastle to Broken Bay (Pittwater) about 38 nm Pittwater is 16 nm north of Sydney Heads Broken Bay to Sydney Harbour about 16 nm Wide, deep, fully open entrance Southport to Coffs is roughly 150 nm, Coffs to Port Stephens 160 nm and the longest single leg, and Port Stephens to Sydney 85 to 110 nm depending on where you finish. A fast motor yacht that leaves the Seaway at first light on the flood can be in Coffs for dinner, Port Stephens the next night, and Sydney Harbour by the third afternoon. Harbours: all-weather or bar The single most useful thing to know about this coast is which entrances you can take in anything and which ones you cannot. No bar, any weather: Sydney Harbour, Newcastle and Port Stephens have wide, deep entrances. Newcastle is a commercial port; keep a listening watch on VHF 9 and 16 and stay clear of the shipping channel. Marine Rescue runs a 24-hour base at Port Stephens. No bar, but watch the entrance: Coffs Harbour. The marina channel is dredged to 4.5 m but sand built up at the entrance faster than expected in 2025, and emergency dredging ran from October; a ten-year dredging programme is proposed. Berths are for 10 to 30 m vessels, rates on enquiry. Designated coastal bars: Ballina, Iluka and Yamba, Port Macquarie, Camden Haven, Forster and Tuncurry, and Swansea at Lake Macquarie. On every one of these NSW law requires every person aboard to wear a lifejacket for the crossing. The official advice is short: cross on an incoming tide, never on the ebb, never without local knowledge, and if in doubt, don’t. Two bars deserve particular respect. Ballina shoals to 3 to 4 m and breaks heavily across the entrance in a large easterly swell; a yacht hit the southern breakwall there in May 2026 and the Marine Rescue vessel that went to help capsized on the bar, with three people lost. Yamba’s bar sits about a mile out and pumps in an east-south-easterly swell, the gap in the Iluka training wall is five metres deep but only wide enough for one and a half boats, and the current through the walls can run more than two knots. Inside, the holding at Iluka is excellent. The NSW Government runs bar webcams at Tweed Heads, Brunswick Heads, Ballina, Evans Head, Iluka and Yamba, Coffs, Nambucca, South West Rocks, Port Macquarie, Camden Haven, Forster, Shoal Bay and Swansea. Watch the full two-minute cycle before you commit. Worth knowing For a 40 to 120 ft motor yacht the simplest plan skips the bars entirely: Seaway, Coffs, Port Stephens or Newcastle, Sydney. Three overnight stops, all of them enterable in the dark and in a blow. Keep Yamba and Forster in reserve for a boat that needs to shorten a leg. Weather and the current The East Australian Current sets south along the shelf at two to three knots and can approach four. North of Port Macquarie it sits five to ten miles offshore; south of Sydney it is thirty or forty miles out. It moves inshore and strengthens in the warm months, weakens and moves offshore in winter. Heading south, find it. Heading home, stay within three to five miles of the coast and inside the 50-metre contour. Wind against current. A fresh southerly blowing against a two-to-three-knot south-setting current builds steep, breaking seas. The bad spots are off Smoky Cape, Seal Rocks and outside Sydney over the canyon. If a southerly is forecast, be in port before it arrives, not fighting it in the current. Southerly busters are the NSW speciality: winds gusting over 29 knots with a temperature drop of at least five degrees inside three hours, mostly October to February, late afternoon or evening after a hot day, often with little cloud to warn you. Sydney averages about five a year and they are strongest between Nowra and Newcastle. Season. Heading south, October onwards is the traditional window, when the northerlies start. East Coast Lows peak in June and July and produce 50 to 80 knots and five-metre seas; another day or two in port is the difference. Forecasts. The Bureau’s coastal waters zones for this trip, north to south: Byron Coast, Coffs Coast, Macquarie Coast, Hunter Coast and Sydney Coast, plus Sydney Enclosed Waters for the harbour and Pittwater. Log on with Marine Rescue NSW by VHF 16, the Marine Rescue app or 02 9471 8300, with destination, people aboard and expected arrival. {{cta}} Fuel Marina diesel prices along the way, as published: Where Diesel Notes Newcastle Cruising Yacht Club $2.878/L on 6 September 2026 24-hour card berth on F Arm; 10% off over 1,000 L, members 12% Sydney: The Spit and Rushcutters Bay (d’Albora) about $2.64/L, undated list Both 24/7; live prices in the d’Albora app, members 20c/L off Sydney: Roseville Bridge, Birkenhead Point $2.68 and $2.52/L, undated list Daytime hours Pittwater: RMYC Broken Bay, The Quays, Holmeport $2.28 to $2.40/L, undated list The Quays fuel wharf takes vessels up to 80 ft Rose Bay Marina, RMYC Point Piper price on the day Rose Bay has a fuel dock and free pump-out; Point Piper fuels 7.30am to 3.30pm Coffs Harbour no diesel berth for a large yacht The new Transport for NSW facility is unleaded only, vessels to 12 m Nelson Bay’s d’Albora fuel wharf runs 24/7 too, price in the app. Plan Coffs as an overnight stop, not a fuel stop, and top up at Newcastle or Port Stephens if you need it before Sydney. A Sunseeker Manhattan 60 burns about 196 litres an hour at 20 knots, so 21 to 26 hours of running is around 4,100 to 5,100 litres; check the range calculation against the longest leg with a third in reserve. Our yacht fuel cost guide puts a dollar figure on each hour. Where to berth in Sydney Every Sydney marina quotes casual berthing on application, so book before you leave the Gold Coast, not when you round the Heads. Marina Takes What is published d’Albora Rushcutters Bay vessels to 40 m, 106 berths casual subject to availability; annual berths reported at $800 to $1,500 a metre d’Albora The Spit, Mosman vessels to 50 m, 203 berths, superyacht berths casual available; 24/7 fuel Cruising Yacht Club of Australia, Rushcutters Bay 213 deep-water berths casual on request via online form Royal Motor Yacht Club, Point Piper members and guests bookings essential; fuel wharf 7.30am to 3.30pm Rose Bay Marina 10 to 37 m, 58 berths casual berthing, pick-up and drop-off, 67 moorings to 16 m Jones Bay Superyacht Marina, Pyrmont 20 m to over 90 m casual and permanent on request Sydney Superyacht Marina, Rozelle alongside to 75 m casual, seasonal and annual on application Royal Prince Alfred, Pittwater vessels to about 30 m 2020 casual rates: 51 to 60 ft $90 a night non-member, larger $100 Newcastle Cruising Yacht Club 180 berths published casual rates from 1 August 2026: 18 m $132 a night, 24 m $166, 30 m $200 For scale, a 24-hour berth for a boat up to 23 m at Sydney Harbour Marina in Cockle Bay was $265 plus $50 shore power in December 2023, against $241 a night for a berth to 25 m at Southport Yacht Club. Sydney annual berths run somewhere between $500 and $2,000 a metre a year depending on where. The NSW rules that catch Queensland boats Registration. A Queensland-registered yacht can cruise NSW without NSW registration provided she is not normally used there, has not been in NSW more than three months, and carries her Queensland numbers and identification plate. After three months you need NSW registration and a NSW licence. Safety gear on open waters. A registered, in-date 406 MHz EPIRB and a marine radio if two nautical miles or more offshore, two orange smoke and two red hand flares, a V-sheet, a fluid-filled compass, a chart, anchor, bilge pump, fire extinguisher, sound signal, waterproof torch, and a lifejacket for everyone. Queensland’s list is close, but check the NSW one before you leave. Lifejackets on bars. Everyone, every designated bar, no exceptions. Sydney Harbour. The Bridge Transit Zone, from Bennelong and Kirribilli Points to Millers and Blues Points, has a 15-knot limit with no anchoring or drifting. Ferries showing an orange diamond have priority; keep 200 m from their bow and 30 m from their sides and stern. Posted limits are usually 4 or 8 knots, sometimes 6, 10 or 15. Sydney VTS works VHF 13 and every vessel on the harbour is required to keep a listening watch. Personal watercraft are banned on the harbour altogether. Run her yourself, or send her down Owners who enjoy the passage make a week of it. Owners who want the boat in Sydney for the summer send her down with a delivery skipper and fly. Published Australian delivery rates: Australian Yacht Deliveries: $650 a day for preparation, plus $5 to $15 per nautical mile depending on the vessel, plus crew travel of $1,500 to $3,500 and fuel. Their worked example is a 15 m yacht over 600 nm in six days for $7,500 excluding fuel. Blue Water Sailing School: $700 a day plus GST for a skipper and one crew, including their travel and provisioning, covering 140 to 200 nm a day on the east coast. Others quote per delivery, typically half up front plus expenses, with the owner’s insurance in force for the trip. Whichever way she goes, the pre-departure list is the same: insurance cruising range confirmed in writing for NSW waters, EPIRB registration current, life raft in date, fuel range checked against the longest leg with a third in hand, spares for impellers, belts and filters, a watch-keeping plan for the overnight legs, AIS on, and the weather window agreed the night before. Making ready — lines, chafe gear and fenders are checked before she leaves, whoever is at the helm. {{product:checklists}} What we do Marine HQ prepares yachts for the run south and back: the pre-departure checks and sea trial, the insurance and registration paperwork, the fuel and spares, the passage plan with the bars marked, and a delivery skipper and crew when the owner would rather meet her in Sydney. Passages further afield work the same way — Fiji, New Caledonia, Indonesia and the wider Pacific — with our delivery crew aboard, or as weather routing and shore support if the owner or their own captain is making the crossing. While she is away her position, fuel and log are in the owner’s MyYacht app, and when she comes home the post-passage service is already booked. Call 0439 748 387 or email yachtsupport@marinehq.com.au and tell us when you want her at Rushcutters Bay.

t: Taking your motor yacht from the Gold Coast to the Whitsundays
d: About 650 nautical miles, three days fast or a fortnight slow. The legs, the Wide Bay Bar and the Great Sandy Strait, fuel stops, Whitsundays marinas and their rates, the Marine Park mooring rules, the season, and what to do before you leave.
x: The legs The Wide Bay Bar and the Strait Season and weather Fuel on the way Where to berth in the Whitsundays The Marine Park rules Before you leave the Seaway Send her, or take her What we do How far is it from the Gold Coast to the Whitsundays by sea? How many days does it take? Do I have to cross the Wide Bay Bar? When is the best time to go? Where can I berth in the Whitsundays and what does it cost? Can I anchor anywhere in the Whitsundays? The run north is the one most Gold Coast owners dream about and fewer make than you would think. It is about 650 nautical miles from the Seaway to Hamilton Island by the usual track, with one bar, one tide-gated strait, a string of good marinas fifty to a hundred miles apart, and the best cruising ground in the country at the end of it. A 20-knot motor yacht does it in three or four days. Here is how to plan it, what it costs on the way, and what the Whitsundays expect of you when you arrive. Key facts - Distance — about 650 nm via Bundaberg, Rosslyn Bay and Mackay; 520 nm in a straight line - Time — about 32 hours’ running at 20 knots, 72 at 9 knots; three to four days fast, six to eight slow, a month if you stop everywhere - The gate — the Wide Bay Bar and the Great Sandy Strait, or go outside Fraser and skip both - Season — May to October; August to early November is best; cyclone season 1 November to 30 April - Berths — Hamilton Island publishes rates ($255 a night for 20 m); Coral Sea Marina and Port of Airlie quote on application; both want $10 million liability cover - Moorings — over 100 free public moorings, colour-banded by size; white pyramid buoys mean no anchoring The legs The track at a glance, Seaway to Airlie Beach. {{map:gold-coast-to-whitsundays}} Leg Distance Notes Gold Coast Seaway to Mooloolaba 82 nm About 4 hours at 20 knots, 8 at 10; strong cross-currents at the Point Cartwright entrance Mooloolaba to the Wide Bay Bar about 70 nm Double Island Point is the only anchorage between, and it is an open roadstead Through the Great Sandy Strait 36 to 40 nm Tide-gated at South White Cliffs and Sheridan Flats; fuel at Urangan Mooloolaba to Bundaberg outside Fraser about 200 nm Round Breaksea Spit; no bar, no gate, one long night Bundaberg to Pancake Creek 66 nm Follow the leads in; sandbanks dry at low water Pancake Creek to Gladstone about 30 nm Or straight on past it Gladstone to Great Keppel and Rosslyn Bay 59 nm plus 10 to 12 Northern Passage saves 20 nm on the shipping channel Rosslyn Bay to Mackay about 250 nm Via the Percy Isles, Pearl Bay or Port Clinton; Middle Percy is the classic stop, 59 nm short of Mackay Mackay to the Whitsundays 17 nm to St Bees, then island hops Airlie Beach to Hamilton Island is 15 to 17 nm The classic plan runs Gold Coast, Mooloolaba, the bar and the Strait, Bundaberg, Pancake Creek, then north in 50 to 60 nm hops. A fast motor yacht leaves the Seaway at first light, fuels at Mooloolaba, takes the bar on the afternoon flood or runs outside overnight, and is at Bundaberg or Pancake Creek on day two, Rosslyn Bay on day three, Mackay or the islands on day four. Letting go — a fast motor yacht leaves the Seaway at first light, with lines and fenders stowed before open water. The Wide Bay Bar and the Strait If you go inside Fraser Island you cross the Wide Bay Bar and then work the tides through the Great Sandy Strait. It is the part of the trip that needs the most planning and the part that goes wrong most often. The bar moves. The waypoints shift tens of metres in a season and are reset after every big swell. The last public figure is from 2017, when the Hook Point light was realigned and the seaward mark moved half a mile north. Since 2022 Maritime Safety Queensland has run virtual AIS buoys on the bar that show on an AIS-equipped plotter and are moved to the deepest water. That alone is a reason to fit AIS before this trip. Ask before you cross. Coast Guard Tin Can Bay, 07 5486 4290 or VHF 16, 67, 80 and 82, six in the morning to six at night, will give you the current marks and tell you what the bar is doing. Log on with them before you go over. Time it. Cross in daylight, in the last two hours of the flood, ideally at high water. On the ebb against a south-easterly swell the bar goes from flat to steep, confused and breaking in minutes. Avoid crossing from seaward in the afternoon with the sun on the leads. The tidal jet off Inskip Point sets you across the line near the inner mark. If in doubt, do not cross. The Strait has two gates. The southern entrance carries 2 to 3 m at low water, South White Cliffs and Ungowa about 1.8 to 2 m, and Sheridan Flats 1.8 to 2.2 m in the marked channel, where the flood tides from north and south meet. A boat drawing 2 m wants half-tide rising at South White Cliffs and mid-tide or better at Sheridan Flats, ideally at slack. Garry’s Anchorage is where you wait. Plan the Strait around neap tides if you can. Or go outside. Run north from Mooloolaba, pass Waddy Point about halfway, round Breaksea Spit and turn for Bundaberg. About 200 nm and a night at sea, no bar, no gate, and a fast motor yacht does it in ten hours. Worth knowing Every July in odd-numbered years, Exercise Talisman Sabre closes about 100 nm of coast from Yeppoon north to the Percy group. In 2025 there was no safe anchorage in that stretch until 17 July, with fines for coming within 500 m of exercise vessels. Talisman Sabre 2027 is being planned now; check the dates before you fix a July departure. Season and weather The Whitsundays run on the trade winds. They re-establish in April and May, the weather settles after June, and the winds ease from mid-September, which makes August to early November the best cruising, with September the month most people name. The dry season, May to October, sits between 20 and 27 degrees. Cyclone season is 1 November to 30 April, and it is not theoretical. Cyclone Koji came ashore between Ayr and Bowen as a category two on 11 January 2026, dropped more than 700 mm on Mackay in 48 hours, and destroyed about 25 boats, most of them on the Airlie Beach moorings against the rock wall. Owners who stayed uninsured were quoted around $8,000 a year for cyclone cover afterwards. Most Gold Coast yachts go north in winter and come home in October or November on the northerlies. Forecast zones north to south: Gold Coast Waters, Sunshine Coast Waters, Hervey Bay Waters, Capricornia Coast and Mackay Coast. {{cta}} Fuel on the way No marina on the route publishes a diesel price online; ring ahead the day before for the price and the wharf hours. Where the fuel is: Stop Diesel Notes Mooloolaba Rockliff’s, Mooloolah River Fisheries, Chippo’s The marina takes vessels to 18 m; rates from 1 July 2026 are $99 a night for 15 m and $118 for 18 m Urangan (Hervey Bay) sheltered diesel wharf The northbound fuelling point after the Strait Bundaberg Port Marina 24/7 self-serve low-flow, high-flow at the commercial wharf 180 berths to 45 m, 3 m at low water, a port of entry Gladstone Marina fuel dock, diesel and petrol 320 vessels; rates from 1 July 2026: 15 m $84 a night, 20 m $108, 27 m $153, first three hours free Keppel Bay Marina, Rosslyn Bay 7am to 5pm weekdays, 9 to 4 weekends 500 berths to 45 m Mackay Marina 24/7 card dock, high-flow 350 to 400 L/min, bulk rates 435 berths including superyacht berths Coral Sea Marina, Airlie booked between 8am and 4.30pm; 24-hour card bowser after hours Commercial traffic has priority at the fuel wharf Hamilton Island 24/7 wharf between F and G arms, low and high flow Vessels to 30 m; call the office first A Sunseeker Manhattan 60 burns about 196 litres an hour at 20 knots, so the 32 hours of running on the way up is around 6,300 litres. Our yacht fuel cost guide puts a dollar figure on each hour. Check the range on the longest leg you intend to run, Rosslyn Bay to Mackay if you do it in one, with a third in reserve. Where to berth in the Whitsundays Marina Takes What is published Coral Sea Marina Resort, Airlie Beach 520 berths, 11 to 80 m, 5 m draft Rates per metre on application; check-in noon, check-out 11am; $10 million liability required; Superyacht Facility of the Year 2026 Hamilton Island Marina 301 berths, superyachts to 45 m Daily monohull: 15 m $180, 18 m $225, 20 m $255, 24 m $325, 27 m $370, 30 m $435; single berth 25% more; day visit 20 to 23 m $175; overnight mooring 15 to 24 m $135; high season June to November; book 24 hours ahead Port of Airlie Marina (d’Albora) 184 berths, to 40 m Rates on application Hayman Island 24 berths to 45 m $350 a day; overnight needs a room booking Shute Harbour ferry and tourism terminal Not a visitor marina; the 395-berth private marina is still “coming soon” Hamilton Island Marina has a 4-knot no-wash limit inside, ferries and barges have priority departing, and there is no anchoring in the cable zone. Both Coral Sea and Hamilton Island want comprehensive cover to replacement value including salvage and clean-up, and $10 million public liability, before you tie up. The Marine Park rules No-anchoring areas are marked by white pyramid buoys with a blue label. Anchoring inside them is an offence and the markers will not hold a boat. Bait Reef and Manta Ray Bay at Hook Island have no buoys at all, only chart boundaries. Public moorings are free, first come, one vessel each, and colour-banded: green for monohulls to 20 m and cats to 18 m, blue to 25 m and 22 m, red to 35 m and 30 m. Limits are two, four or 24 hours between 7am and 5pm; pick one up at or after 3pm and you can stay until 9am. There are more than 100 across the islands, including 14 at Tongue Bay for the walk to the Hill Inlet lookout. Whitehaven Beach sits in a green Marine National Park zone: no personal watercraft, transit at no wake, camping only with a permit. Anchor in sand or mud, well clear of coral, at five to one scope. Recreational vessels up to 20 m can anchor in every setting; larger yachts are restricted in the most protected ones. Permits and charges. The Marine Park environmental charge applies to commercial operators, not private yachts. Before you leave the Seaway Insurance. Club Marine and Nautilus cover to 250 nm offshore, which is fine; the question is cyclone season. Pantaenius loads Queensland cruising about 10% for named-storm cover and wants a written contingency plan for yachts under 80 ft. Confirm the cruising range and the cyclone clause in writing. EPIRB, flares, life raft. A 406 MHz EPIRB registered with AMSA, two orange smoke and two red hand flares in date, and a life raft with a current service. AIS. Transmitting Class B with an MMSI. It is how you see the shipping off Gladstone and Mackay, and how you see the virtual buoys on the Wide Bay Bar. Fuel range. Longest leg plus a third, with the generator's burn at anchor added in. Spares. Impellers, belts, filters, an anode set, and the tools to fit them; the nearest dealer is a long way from Pancake Creek. Comms. Coverage is thin between Bundaberg and Mackay. Starlink Roam is $85 a month for 100 GB in Australia and the hardware is $399. Watch-keeping. A plan for the overnight legs with two people awake, and the weather window agreed the night before each leg. The marinas. Book Coral Sea or Hamilton Island before you leave, with the insurance certificate ready to send. {{product:checklists}} Send her, or take her Owners who love the passage make a fortnight of it. Owners who want their boat waiting on a mooring at Hamilton Island send her up. Published Australian delivery rates are $650 a day for preparation plus $5 to $15 a nautical mile with crew travel of $1,500 to $3,500 and fuel on top, or $700 a day plus GST for a skipper and one crew covering 140 to 200 nm a day. The published example is $7,500 excluding fuel for a 15 m yacht over 600 nm in six days. What we do Marine HQ prepares yachts for the season north: the pre-departure service and sea trial, insurance and cyclone-clause paperwork, fuel and spares, a passage plan with the bar and the Strait tides worked out, and a delivery skipper and crew when the owner would rather fly. The same applies further afield: we plan and support international passages — Fiji, New Caledonia, Indonesia and the wider Pacific — either with our own delivery crew aboard, or as weather routing and shore support for an owner or captain making the crossing themselves. While she is away her position, fuel and log sit in the owner’s MyYacht app, and the post-season haul-out is booked for when she comes home. Call 0439 748 387 or email yachtsupport@marinehq.com.au and tell us which month you want to be at Whitehaven.

t: What size boat should I get? Choosing a motor yacht for the Gold Coast
d: The four questions that decide length, what each ten feet buys you in cabins and tankage, how every running cost scales with size, the Gold Coast depth and marina limits, the insurers' ten-foot rule, and new-boat price bands with dates.
x: The four questions What each ten feet buys you How the running costs scale What the Gold Coast decides for you The ten-foot rule Hull type and range What it costs to buy Before you decide What we do What size motor yacht suits a couple on the Gold Coast? What size boat do I need for a family of four? How much more does ten extra feet cost to run? Is a 60 ft boat too big for a first boat? Which sizes hold their value best? Can I take a 50-footer to the Whitsundays? The honest answer is that length is the last thing to decide, not the first. Four questions settle it: how you will use her, who sleeps aboard, where she will live, and who will drive her. Answer those and the size falls out, along with the budget to run her, which on the Gold Coast is roughly 10 to 15% of her value a year. For most owner-operators here the answer lands between 50 and 65 ft . Here is why, what each ten feet buys and costs, and where the Gold Coast itself sets limits. Key facts - The four questions — use, people aboard overnight, where she lives, who drives - The couple’s ceiling — 60 to 65 ft comfortable, 70 to 75 ft the stretch, above 75 ft almost always crewed - Three cabins — from about 55 ft in the luxury production boats; four cabins from about 65 ft - Berth by length — Southport Yacht Club member rate: 49 ft $10,230 a year, 59 ft $16,087, 66 ft $23,954, 73 ft $29,308, 82 ft $38,226 - The insurers’ ten-foot rule — experience on a boat within about ten feet of the one you are buying, or a captain signs you off - Running costs — 10 to 15% of value a year is the Australian brokers’ rule of thumb The four questions Every credible buying guide, from the yacht brokers to Club Marine to Boat Gold Coast, comes back to the same four. How will you use her? Day runs to the Broadwater and Wave Break, weekends at anchor at Tipplers or Moreton Bay, a fortnight up the coast each winter, or the Whitsundays every season. Day boating is happy at 40 ft. Weekends want proper cabins, a galley and enclosed heads. Coastal cruising wants tankage, storage and a hull that behaves in a following sea. Who is aboard overnight? Count beds, not deck chairs. A couple who host day guests need one great cabin and a big cockpit. A family of four who also bring friends need three cabins and two heads, which is a 50 ft boat, not a 45. Where will she live? The berth sets the length as surely as the budget does. Dry stacks on the Gold Coast stop at about 10 m. Marina berths come in bands, and the jump from a 59 ft berth to a 66 ft berth at Southport is $7,900 a year. Who drives her? If the answer is you, the honest ceiling for a couple is 60 to 65 ft, 70 to 75 with pods, thrusters and practice. Above that you are hiring a captain, and the boat's cost changes character. Our crew guide has the numbers. Worth knowing Boat Gold Coast’s advice is the least glamorous and the most useful: sit down with your family first and agree who will use the boat, where it will go and what you will actually do on it, before you look at a single listing. The size argument usually ends there. What each ten feet buys you The luxury production boats make the bands easy to see. Volume grows with the cube of length, so a 60-footer is not a fifth bigger than a 50; owners who have done it describe the 50 as three times the boat. Length Yacht Cabins Beam Fuel and water Who runs her 54 ft Sunseeker Predator 50 2 cabins, room for a tender behind the transom 4.48 m 1,800 L / 430 L Owner, easily 58 ft Princess F55 3 cabins plus a crew cabin, 2 bathrooms 4.87 m 2,750 L / 608 L Owner 64 ft Sunseeker Manhattan 60 3 en suite cabins plus crew quarters 5.0 m 3,000 L / 700 L Owner, or day crew 66 ft Princess F65 4 cabins 5.10 m 4,100 L / not stated Owner with help, or captain 71 ft Azimut S7 4 staterooms plus a crew cabin not stated about 3,800 L / not stated Captain, or a very experienced owner 77 ft Sunseeker 76 Yacht 4 cabins plus a crew cabin 5.95 m 6,000 L / 1,400 L Captain Lengths are each builder’s or reviewer’s length overall (the 76 Yacht’s 23.6 m includes the pulpit). The Azimut S7’s tank is 1,004 US gallons in Yachting magazine’s review, converted here. Where a review did not state a figure, the table says so. Two things move with length that buyers underestimate. The tender grows with the boat: a swim-platform tender is about 3 m on a 12 to 15 m yacht and 3.5 m on a 20 to 25 m yacht, and the Predator 50 has room for a Williams 325 behind the transom, the Azimut S7 carries its tender in a garage under the sun pad, and the Pershing GTX80’s hydraulic platform takes a Williams 345. The systems grow with it: air conditioning on a boat this size means a generator, and the gyro that stops her rolling at anchor is a Seakeeper 10 on a 50 to 60 ft boat, list price about US$127,000 before installation, and a Seakeeper 18 at 60 to 75 ft. Use decides length — a boat for the Broadwater and a boat for the Whitsundays are different boats, and so are the berths they fit. How the running costs scale Every line scales with length, and some scale faster than length. At Berth, SYC member, a year Fuel burn at cruise, from sea trials and builder’s figures Antifoul Crew 49 ft $10,230 Not published for a luxury boat this size; see the 55 ft row GCCM package from $89.50 a foot to 50 ft, about $4,400 Owner 55 ft $16,087 (59 ft double) Princess F55 (58 ft): about 215 L/h at 23 to 24 knots; Sunseeker Predator 50 (54 ft): 167 L/h at 20 knots Quote only above 50 ft Owner 60 ft $19,311 (59 ft single) Sunseeker Manhattan 60 (64 ft): 196 L/h at 20 knots, 256 at 23.6; Grand Banks 60: 86 L/h at 15 knots, 228 at 25 Quote; allow around $10,000 all in Owner or day crew 65 ft $23,954 (66 ft) Princess F65 (66 ft): 274 L/h at 21 knots; Palm Beach 65: 165 L/h at 25 knots Quote Owner with help 68 to 73 ft $29,308 (73 ft) Azimut S7 (71 ft): 245 L/h at 24.8 knots, 326 at 28.9 Quote Captain likely 82 ft $38,226 Sunseeker 76 Yacht (76 ft, builder’s figures): 290 L/h at 23 knots; Pershing GTX80: 439 L/h at 28 knots; nothing we trust is published above 80 ft Quote Captain and crew From 80 to 120 ft the numbers stop being published and the rules change. Southport quotes berths over 82 ft on application; GCCM’s 2022 schedule had 91–100 ft at $5,000 a month and 101–110 ft at $6,000. Published guidance is that a crew member is recommended from about 79 ft and a professional crew above about 98 ft, and the Crew Pacific guide puts a captain on a 100 to 120 ft yacht at $10,000 to $14,000 a month including super. At this size the question is less which boat than who runs her, which is our crew guide. Southport Yacht Club is the only Gold Coast marina with a published rate card; the others quote, and the resort marinas cost more. Visitor rates at Southport are 40 to 50% above member rates. Insurance follows the sum insured, so it scales with price rather than length, at somewhere between 1 and 3% of value a year. The 10% rule of thumb holds well for a new owner-operated boat under warranty and understates an older or larger one, which is why Australian brokers say 10 to 15%. Our cost-of-ownership guide builds the whole bill for a 60-footer. What the Gold Coast decides for you Water. The Coomera River channel to the marine precinct carries about 3.0 m; the published guideline for the run from the Seaway is a 2.1 m draught without a pilot, 3 m to Southport Yacht Club. Every boat in the table above fits, but a deep-keeled displacement boat wants the tide up the river. Speed. Six knots for vessels 6.5 m and over from Paradise Point up the Coomera River, so a Coomera berth means an hour and a half each way at displacement speed whatever you own. Bridges. Sovereign Islands 5.0 m, Ephraim Island 5.9 m, the Sundale Bridge 4.5 m at highest tide. A flybridge boat does not go under any of them; plan the berth accordingly. Berths. Runaway Bay to 30 m, Hope Harbour to 40 m, Sanctuary Cove to 65 m, Southport to 130 m. Dry stack to about 10 m or 14 tonnes at GCCM, so nothing in this guide goes in a shed for the season. The Seaway. The safest bar in south-east Queensland, but nasty on the ebb against a swell. A 50-footer and a 75-footer cross it the same way: on the flood, logged on with Seaway Tower. The ten-foot rule Underwriters look for experience on a boat no more than about ten feet shorter than the one they are insuring. A 40 to 50 step is normal; 25 to 50 is not. Above the jump they attach a condition: a professional captain aboard until they sign you off, anywhere from a week to a season. Insurers count boats you have owned, not boats you have driven. Owners who have made the jump say the same thing on every forum: step up in stages, or charter the size first. Docking a 60-footer with pods and a joystick is easier than docking a 40-footer with shafts, but the boat itself, the systems, the yard bills and the hours of upkeep are what change, and they change by the cube. {{cta}} Hull type and range A planing hull gets you to Moreton Bay for lunch; a displacement hull gets you to the Whitsundays on a third of the fuel. Full-displacement boats cruise at 6 to 9 knots, semi-displacement at 10 to 16 and beyond with power, and planing boats’ running costs are commonly 50 to 150% higher than a displacement boat of the same length. The Grand Banks 60 shows the trade: 2,000 nm at 10 knots, 636 nm at 25. A Princess F65 carries 4,100 litres for about 252 nm at 21 knots, and Yachting magazine’s Pershing GTX80 test gives 300 nm at 28 knots, with nearly double that at slow cruise. If the plan is a season north, tankage and range at the speed you will actually run matter more than the length. What it costs to buy Published prices from tests, reviews and listing sites, in the currency and year each was quoted, so you can see the bands. The Sunseeker Predator 75 and 76 Yacht rows are dealer asking prices, which move, so each carries its date. Boat Length Published price When Sunseeker Predator 75 75 ft $7.99 million (2025 boat, NSW dealer) to $8.4 million (2026 boat), new, asking Australian listing sites, October 2026 Sunseeker 76 Yacht 77 ft used, asking: US$2.4 million to US$4.9 million, average US$3.9 million YachtBuyer listings, October 2026 Azimut S7 71 ft from €2.75 million, the price given for the 2023 premiere (not a current offer) ilodka, 2023 premiere Sunseeker Predator 50 54 ft from £810,000 including VAT (UK) review published March 2019 Princess F55 58 ft $3.49 million base, $3.79 million as tested May 2023 Sunseeker Manhattan 60 64 ft about $3 million, depending on options Trade-A-Boat review, undated Grand Banks 60 60 ft $4.13 million base, $4.5 million as tested 2018 Palm Beach 65 65 ft about $4.2 million as tested 2018 Princess F65 66 ft £3.3 million as tested including VAT (UK) review published March 2023 The UK prices are in pounds and include VAT, so they are a guide to the band, not an Australian price. The Manhattan 60 review gives no currency or date for its figure, and the 76 Yacht figures are US-dollar asking prices from listings worldwide, mostly boats between six and nine years old. Depreciation runs roughly 10 to 20% in the first year, 30 to 40% by year three and 40 to 50% by year five, then flattens. That is the case for a three to five year old boat: the big hit is taken, the warranty may still have life, and the survey tells you what you are buying. The Australian luxury segment gained share in late 2025 while trailer boats fell. Brokers put the deepest demand in the 30 to 70 ft power range, so a well-kept boat in this band is also the easiest to sell when you move up. Two schools of thought on the first boat, and both are right for someone. “Buy your second boat first” skips the starter boat you will outgrow in a year. “Start small” makes sure you like it before you commit. The compromise most experienced owners land on is a boat one size below the dream, run for two seasons, with the records kept so she sells well. {{product:calculator}} Before you decide Sea-trial her on a choppy day with the people who will normally be aboard, not on a flat morning with the broker. Ask the twenty questions the brokers publish: engine hours, last major service, last antifoul, fuel burn at cruise, how she handles in a tight marina, what berth she needs, and what she costs a year. Add 5 to 12% to the purchase price for survey, registration, first-year insurance and the berth deposit. Walk the berth you can actually get before you sign. On the Gold Coast the berth, not the boat, is often the constraint. Budget the running costs at 10 to 15% and see whether the bigger boat still fits the number. What we do Marine HQ’s pre-purchase consultation is exactly this conversation with your shortlist in front of us: what each boat will cost to berth, antifoul, insure, fuel and crew on the Gold Coast, whether you can run her yourself, and what the survey and sea trial should look for on that particular model.
