t: Yacht fuel cost: what a 70–80 ft luxury yacht burns (2026)
d: What Sunseeker, Azimut and Pershing motor yachts of 70 to 80 ft burn at slow, fast and top speed, and what that costs at October 2026 diesel prices.
x: The short answer What diesel costs today What a luxury motor yacht burns Two Sunseekers Slow versus fast: what 100 hours costs What a full tank is worth How to work out your own number Where fuel money goes What we do about it How much fuel does a 70 to 80 ft luxury motor yacht use per hour? How much does it cost to fill a luxury yacht's fuel tanks? Is it cheaper to run a luxury motor yacht slowly? How much fuel does a 74 ft Sunseeker use? What is the diesel price on the Gold Coast? How do I work out what a trip will cost in fuel? Why do published fuel figures differ between boats of the same length? A 70 to 80 ft luxury motor yacht burns about 50 to 70 litres an hour at 10 to 12 knots, and 330 to 490 litres an hour at 28 knots . At the October 2026 diesel price of $3.24 a litre, that is $162 to $221 an hour slow and $1,056 to $1,575 an hour fast . Speed is the biggest thing you control, and this guide shows what it costs, boat by boat, using published figures for Azimut, Pershing and Sunseeker. Key facts — October 2026 - Diesel — $3.19 a litre for members, $3.24 for non-members, at the Royal Queensland Yacht Squadron on 1 October - 71 ft Azimut S7 — about 245 L/h at 24.8 knots, 326 L/h at 28.9 knots - Pershing GTX80 — about 68 L/h at 10 knots, 439 L/h at 28 knots - 74 ft Sunseeker 74 Sport Yacht — about 50 L/h at 12 knots, 486 L/h at 28 knots (builder’s figures) - Per nautical mile — slowing to 10 or 12 knots cuts the fuel cost per mile by more than half on the Pershing and the Sunseeker The short answer $3.24/L diesel, 1 October 2026, non-member price +14% on the 3 September price, in four weeks $1,423/hr Pershing GTX80 at 28 knots $16,521 to fill a Pershing GTX80 from empty Fuel is the cost that moves with how much you use the boat. The berth, insurance and registration arrive on the same dates whether she leaves the pen or not. Fuel doesn’t, and the price per litre has moved sharply this spring. If you are budgeting a year, our guide to the cost of owning a yacht on the Gold Coast puts fuel in context with every other line. What diesel costs today No Gold Coast marina we found publishes its pump price. The nearest published price is the Royal Queensland Yacht Squadron’s, in Brisbane, updated on 1 October 2026: Fuel Members Non-members Premium diesel $3.19 a litre $3.24 a litre Premium unleaded $3.00 a litre $3.05 a litre A month earlier, on 3 September, the same club listed diesel at $2.79 to $2.84 a litre. That is about 14% more in four weeks. Every dollar figure below uses $3.24 a litre , the non-member price, so it is the cautious end. Ask your own fuel dock for today’s price, and date any number you rely on. What a luxury motor yacht burns Two of the boats below were run by Yachting magazine, which reports speed and fuel flow at each engine setting. Its figures are in US gallons an hour, which we have converted at 3.785 litres to the gallon. Both boats have three engines with pod drives. Yacht Engines Speed Burn Cost an hour Cost a nautical mile Azimut S7 (71 ft) Three Volvo Penta D13 IPS1050, 800 hp each 24.8 knots 245 L/h $794 $32 28.9 knots 326 L/h $1,056 $37 36.3 knots (top) 466 L/h $1,510 $42 Pershing GTX80 Three Volvo Penta D13 IPS1350, 1,000 hp each 10 knots 68 L/h $221 $22 28 knots 439 L/h $1,423 $51 Yachting printed these as three data points in the text, not a full table, and the Azimut test did not state its load. The Pershing’s top speed was 33.6 knots at 2,475 rpm, but the review gives no fuel figure for it. The Azimut was run in calm water off Cannes in the early morning. Main engines and fuel filters. A generator running at anchor burns fuel that never shows up in a speed-and-burn table. Two Sunseekers Independent sea-trial tables for a Sunseeker of 74 to 76 ft are hard to find. The best published figures are the builder’s own numbers, as listed by YachtBuyer. They are not independent sea trials, and the page does not say what load, weather or sea state they were measured in. We have used them because they are what is published; treat them as a guide to the size of the bill. Yacht Engines Speed Burn Cost an hour Cost a nautical mile Sunseeker 74 Sport Yacht (74 ft) Twin MAN V12, 1,550 hp 12 knots 50 L/h $162 $14 28 knots 486 L/h $1,575 $56 34 knots (top) 565 L/h $1,831 $54 Sunseeker 76 Yacht (76 ft) Twin MAN V12, 1,550 hp 23 knots 290 L/h $940 $41 31 knots (top) 600 L/h $1,944 $63 The 76 Yacht’s listing gives a 10 knot range of 500 nautical miles but no burn figure at that speed, so there is no slow-speed row for it. Above about 80 ft we found no published burn figure we could trust; ask the builder for the fuel curve for your engines. Three things stand out. Slow is a different cost entirely. The Pershing at 10 knots costs $221 an hour. At 28 knots it costs $1,423, over six times as much, to cover 2.8 times the distance. The last few knots cost the most. The Azimut S7 burns 140 more litres an hour going from 28.9 to 36.3 knots, and the Sunseeker 74 costs $256 an hour more at 34 knots than at 28. Your boat will not match these. Engines, load, weather, sea state and hull condition all move every number. Slow versus fast: what 100 hours costs The same 100 hours underway on each boat, at the lowest and highest speeds published for it. Yacht 100 hours at the lower speed 100 hours at the higher speed The difference Pershing GTX80 (10 and 28 knots) $22,077 $142,271 $120,194 Sunseeker 74 Sport Yacht (12 and 28 knots, builder’s figures) $16,200 $157,464 $141,264 Azimut S7 (24.8 and 28.9 knots) $79,353 $105,599 $26,246 Sunseeker 76 Yacht (23 and 31 knots, builder’s figures) $93,960 $194,400 $100,440 The throttle is the biggest fuel decision. On the Pershing GTX80 test, 10 knots cost $221 an hour and 28 knots cost $1,423. A hundred hours at 28 knots is not a hundred hours at the same distance. At 28 knots the Pershing covers about 2,800 nautical miles in 100 hours; at 10 knots it covers 1,000. Fuel is the cost of the hour, which is why the cost per mile in the tables above is the fairer comparison. Budget trap Most owners quote a fuel figure from a brochure or a broker. Ask which speed it was measured at. The number at 10 knots and the number at 28 knots can differ by more than a factor of six. What a full tank is worth Fuel capacity tells you what a fill costs and how far she can go. From the same two tests: Yacht Tank capacity Cost to fill from empty at $3.24 Azimut S7 1,004 US gal (about 3,801 L) $12,314 Pershing GTX80 1,347 US gal (about 5,099 L) $16,521 {{cta}} How to work out your own number You need three things: the litres an hour at the speed you will run, the hours underway, and the price a litre. Litres an hour. Ask the builder or your engineer for the fuel curve for your engines, or look up a published sea trial for your model. Hours underway. Count only the engine hours, not the time at the dock. Price a litre. Use today’s price from your fuel dock, and add a margin because the price has moved this spring. For example, a Pershing GTX80 on a two-hour run at 28 knots: 439 litres an hour × 2 hours × $3.24 = $2,845 . The same two hours at 10 knots cover about a third of the distance and cost 68 × 2 × $3.24 = $441 . Two things the tables do not include. The generator burns fuel at anchor and overnight, and a speed-and-burn table says nothing about a night at a mooring. And a hull with growth on it burns more at the same speed; our antifouling guide covers how often the Gold Coast’s warm water makes that necessary. {{product:calculator}} Where fuel money goes Speed, not distance. The Pershing’s cost per mile at 28 knots is more than double its cost at 10 knots, and the Sunseeker 74’s is about four times. Price timing. Diesel rose about 14% between September and October 2026. A trip priced a month ago is not the trip you pay for now. Filling from empty. A full tank is a five-figure cheque on a boat this size. Pay attention to when you fill, not only how much. A fouled hull. A hull with growth burns more fuel at the same speed, so part of the antifoul pays for itself. Generator and hotel loads. Air conditioning and a generator running at a weekend anchorage add litres the speed tables do not show. What we do about it Marine HQ runs the maintenance for motor yachts across the Gold Coast, and fuel is part of how we keep owners informed. For each trip we record the litres taken on at the start and the litres put back at the end, so the owner sees what the trip actually cost, in litres and in dollars, not a guess. It also shows early when a boat starts burning more than she should, which is usually a fouled hull or an engine due for service. If you are weighing up a purchase or want a straight fuel budget for the boat you already own, call us on 0439 748 387 or email yachtsupport@marinehq.com.au.

t: The annual haul-out: a checklist for what should happen while your yacht is out of the water
d: Marine HQ's standard annual out-of-water scope for a motor yacht, section by section: hull, running gear, engines, stabilisers, safety, electrical, systems and tender, and what to ask for in writing.
x: Before the lift: the sea trial Hull and underwater Topsides and presentation Engines and machinery Stabilisers, thrusters and steering Safety and compliance Electrical and electronics Systems and comfort Tender and toys What goes wrong, and how to stop it What we do How often should a motor yacht be hauled out? How long does the annual haul-out take? What is a pre-haul sea trial for? Do I need to be there? What usually gets added to the scope once she is out? What should I get in writing? A haul-out is the one time each year you can see the whole boat. Most yards will sell you an antifoul; the value is in everything else that can only be checked, serviced or replaced while she is on the hardstand. This is the standard annual scope Marine HQ runs on every managed motor yacht, in the order the yard works through it, with what to ask for at each step. Key facts - When — once a year in Gold Coast water, timed with the antifoul - How long — three to five days for antifoul only; one to two weeks for the full annual scope - Book — four to six weeks ahead; longer heading into summer and before the May boat show - Start with — a pre-haul sea trial, so problems are measured under load before she comes out - Rule — nothing is added to the scope without a priced line and your approval - Record — photographs of everything found, and the paint, litres and anode sizes written down for next year Before the lift: the sea trial Once she is on blocks nothing can be run under load, so the diagnostic happens on the way to the yard. A short run at cruise with the engine room open tells you what the annual service needs to include. Engine and gearbox temperatures at cruise and at wide-open throttle, against last year’s. Exhaust colour and smoke on acceleration. Vibration through the rev range, which points at props, shafts, cutless bearings or mounts. Shaft-seal drip rate at speed and at rest. Stabiliser, thruster and steering behaviour, and any hydraulic noise. A note of the engine and generator hours, because the service schedule runs on hours or calendar, whichever comes first. Hull and underwater Haul out and high-pressure wash. Done on a wash-down pad that captures the run-off; the yard's environmental levy pays for that. Photograph the hull before the wash if the growth tells a story. Full hull inspection and report. Blisters, moisture readings on an older hull, gelcoat damage, keel and chine condition. This is the step that decides whether the antifoul is a straight recoat or a bigger job. Antifoul, full application. Two coats, a third on the waterline and leading edges, the brand and litres named in the quote. The whole antifouling job, prices included, is in our antifouling guide. Anodes renewed. Hull, shaft, rudder and trim tabs. Photograph the old ones next to the new; how far they have gone tells you whether the boat's bonding is doing its job. Propellers. Inspect, clean, check for corrosion and dings, Propspeed. A prop scan and repitch is a separate job if the sea trial showed vibration. Shafts, cutless bearings, P-brackets and stern glands. Lift the shaft and feel for play. A worn cutless bearing is the most common thing added to a scope on the hardstand. Through-hulls and seacocks. Every one exercised, serviced and checked for corrosion. A seacock that will not turn is a boat that cannot be saved from a burst hose. Rudders and bearings. Check for play and for water in the rudder. Thruster tunnels. Cleaned, anodes replaced, props checked. Topsides and presentation While she is out and the yard has staging up, the hull is at the right height for the work that is awkward in the water. Topsides cut, polish and wax. Hull and superstructure detail. Teak decks cleaned, caulking inspected, treated. Stainless and metalwork polished. Full interior detail, if it is scheduled for this visit. Engines and machinery The annual services fall due here because the boat is idle and the trades are on site. Volvo Penta, MAN, MTU and Caterpillar all set intervals on hours or calendar time, whichever comes first, so a low-hours year is still a service year. Main engines: annual service, oil and filters, plus whatever the hours call for. The 500-hour and 1,000-hour services add injectors, aftercoolers and heat exchangers and should be quoted before the lift, not discovered during it. Generators: annual service. Raw-water impellers renewed. Belts, hoses and coolant inspected or renewed. Sea strainers cleaned. Engine mounts and bilges inspected. Stabilisers, thrusters and steering Stabiliser annual service, Seakeeper or fin. On a fin system the fin seals and actuators are checked from outside while she is out. Bow and stern thrusters serviced, anodes replaced. Steering and hydraulics inspected and bled. {{cta}} Safety and compliance Out of the water is the natural point to bring every certificate and expiry into line, because the gear is being handled anyway. Life raft serviced and recertified. EPIRB battery checked and the AMSA registration current. Fire extinguishers and engine-room suppression serviced and tagged. Flares checked for expiry and replaced. Life jackets and safety gear inspected. Bilge pumps, float switches and the high-water alarm tested. First-aid kit restocked. Worth knowing Keep the paint invoice, the slipway receipt and the anode sizes. The national biofouling guidelines ask for them, insurers like them at claim time, and next year’s yard will quote faster with them. Electrical and electronics Battery banks load-tested and inspected. Navigation, anchor and deck lights tested. Electronics and multifunction displays updated, software and charts. Shore power, inverter and charger checked. Wiring and connections inspected, especially in the engine room and lazarette. Systems and comfort Air-conditioning serviced and gas checked. Watermaker serviced and filters changed, if fitted. Fresh, grey and black water systems and the calorifier checked. Heads and sanitation serviced. Gas system leak-tested, if fitted. Tender and toys Tender engine serviced and hull checked. Davit and lifting gear inspected and load-tested. Water toys and equipment checked. Tender — the outboard is serviced and the hull checked while the yacht is in the yard. {{product:haul-out}} {{product:launch-sea-trial}} What goes wrong, and how to stop it The scope grows on the hardstand. It always does; the question is whether each addition arrives as a priced line for your approval or as a surprise on the invoice. Insist on the former. The paint goes on before the inspection is finished. Then the seacock that needed replacing gets painted over. Inspection first, paint last. Nobody photographs anything. A photo of the old anode, the worn bearing and the blister is what lets you approve work from your phone and lets the next yard see what was done. The relaunch is “when it’s done”. Book it. A boat waiting on one part sits on the hardstand at a daily rate. The schedule lives in someone’s head. Write down the hours, the paint, the litres, the anode sizes and the dates, so next year’s scope starts from a record rather than a memory. What we do This checklist is Marine HQ’s baseline; every managed yacht also carries her own additional items for her make, systems and age on her individual schedule. We run the sea trial, write the scope, get every line quoted, book the lift and the relaunch, and have someone on the hardstand while the work is done. Every finding is photographed into the owner’s MyYacht app, nothing proceeds without approval of the scope and quote, and the record goes straight into her maintenance history so next year is booked before it is due. If hers is coming up, call 0439 748 387 or email yachtsupport@marinehq.com.au.

t: Detailing and ceramic coating for a motor yacht on the Gold Coast: what it costs, how long it lasts, and what's in the job
d: Wash-downs, cut and polish, wax versus sealant versus ceramic, gelcoat versus paint, teak and stainless, with the published Australian prices, the Queensland sun and salt factors, and Marine HQ's own wash-down routine.
x: Why the Gold Coast is hard on a boat The wash-down: what a proper one includes Wax, sealant or ceramic Gelcoat versus paint Teak, stainless and clears What it costs The rules What to check before you pay for it What we do How much does boat detailing cost on the Gold Coast? How often should a yacht be washed on the Gold Coast? Is ceramic coating worth it on a boat? Can you cut and polish a painted hull? What's the right way to look after teak decks? Why does my stainless get brown spots? Gold Coast sun sits at the top of the UV scale for most of the year, the water is salt, and the Coomera River carries silt. A motor yacht here loses her shine faster than almost anywhere in the country, which is why detailing is not a luxury line on the budget but the thing that decides what she looks like at survey and what she is worth at sale. Here is what the work involves, what each layer of protection really lasts, what the published prices are, and the wash-down routine our own crew run every week. Key facts - Wash — fresh rinse within 24 hours of every salt trip; full pH-neutral wash every two to four weeks - Protection — wax two to three months; sealant six to twelve; professional ceramic 18 to 36 months with top-ups - Prices — no Gold Coast detailer publishes rates; Sydney’s published card is $5 a foot to wash, $20 a foot to machine polish - Ceramic — no Australian price published for a 40 to 120 ft yacht; the preparation is most of the cost - Gelcoat or paint — gelcoat can be cut; Awlgrip and Alexseal cannot, or not much - Teak — never sanded as routine; sealed, not oiled; re-coat when it stops beading Why the Gold Coast is hard on a boat UV. The Bureau’s averages put January at UV 11 or higher over almost all of Australia, and Brisbane needs sun protection every month of the year. Gelcoat chalks, paint fades, clears yellow, and it happens faster on dark hulls. Salt. A wet berth means salt air around the clock. The stainless standard body puts tea staining as most likely within five kilometres of surf or a few hundred metres of still salt water, which describes every marina on the Coast. Silt. The Coomera River runs at up to 100 NTU of turbidity after floods and higher upstream. A boat in the Coomera precinct wears a brown line at the waterline that a Broadwater boat does not. Birds. Uric acid etches gelcoat within minutes in sun. Left for a week, the mark needs compounding out. The kit — machine, graded pads and clean cloths; the pad and compound are matched to the surface, not the other way round. Cut and polish — the least aggressive step that removes the oxidation, and no more. The wash-down: what a proper one includes This is the Marine HQ crew routine, the one on the clipboard on every managed yacht. A wash-down is also our regular close-up inspection, which is why it ends with a report. Before you start. Check the wind and the sun; avoid a strong breeze or full hot sun. Remove covers and cushions and stow them dry. Open and air the lockers. Fresh shore water connected, pH-neutral boat soap only, dedicated cloths for glass and clears, every hatch and port closed. No harsh brushes on gelcoat, glass or clears. Rinse, top down. Flush the whole vessel with fresh water from the top before anything touches her. Salt and grit lifted off first are salt and grit not ground in. Wash section by section. Hardtop, flybridge and arch; superstructure and cabin sides; hull topsides and boot stripe. Work in shade, soft mitt or soft brush, rinse each section before it dries. Decks and non-skid. Soft deck brush and soap, rinse thoroughly, clear the scuppers and drains. Glass and clears. Glass with a dedicated cleaner and a clean cloth. Clears and isinglass with fresh water and a soft cloth only, no chemicals, no scrubbing. Windex, Rain-X and ammonia products void the clears' warranty. Stainless. Rinse and wipe every rail, fitting and cleat. Spot-polish and protect as required. Report any rust or corrosion. Teak. Rinse well. A light scrub across the grain only if needed, never aggressive, and protect the caulking. Chamois. Gelcoat, glass and stainless, to stop water spots, especially on dark surfaces and glass. Tender and aft deck. Rinse and wipe the tender, wash the cockpit and aft deck, check the drains. Covers, cushions, lockers. Refit once dry with ventilation underneath; wash covers where needed; clean and air lockers then secure them. Pack down. Hoses coiled, mops and mitts hung to dry, buckets rinsed, gear back where it lives. Finish and report. A final walk-around for damage, corrosion, leaks and loose fittings; any issue photographed and reported; the wash logged with date and crew. {{product:checklists}} How often: a fresh-water rinse within 24 hours of every salt trip, and a full wash every two to four weeks in season, more for a wet-berthed boat than a dry-stored one. Dry stacks stop at about 10 m, so for a 40 to 120 ft yacht the choice is a wet berth with a good routine, or a shed for the yard period. {{cta}} Wax, sealant or ceramic Layer Lasts Cost, published Upkeep Wax two to three months; one-step cleaner waxes about six Sydney rate $3.50 a foot added to a wash on a 51 to 60 ft boat Reapply every few months; easy, cheap, short Polymer sealant six to twelve months Quoted with a polish Re-coat two or three times a year on painted hulls Ceramic, spray-on three to six months From $7.70 for a 50 mL bottle, applied after a wash A maintenance layer, not a coating Ceramic, professional 18 to 36 months claimed; 30-month field tests still beading No Australian price for a large yacht; jet skis from $650, trailer boats from $850 pH-neutral washes only, no wax over it, booster spray every three to four months, annual inspection The manufacturers’ own numbers are the honest ones. Kovalent, the coating used by one Coomera applicator, says 24 to 36 months, with the three-to-five-year warranty conditional on maintenance by an approved applicator. Glidecoat says 18 months for its standard product and two years for its premium one, and its own 30-month Florida study showed gloss readings still between 50 and 85 with water beading. Gtechniq’s spray-on Fast Coat is rated at up to six months. Independent reviewers put professional ceramic at 18 to 24 months in southern-US conditions, which are the nearest thing to Queensland, with a touch-up rather than a full recoat each year. Worth knowing Ceramic is only as good as the preparation. The hull has to be stripped of every trace of wax, decontaminated, compounded and polished before the coating goes on, and any swirl or scratch left behind is locked in under it. That preparation is most of the job and most of the price. A ceramic quote that is cheaper than a cut and polish has skipped the cut and polish. Ceramic Pro Australia’s own page says what the coating does not do: it does not remove the need for wash-downs, and it does not fully prevent salt, water spots or marine growth. What it does is make the wash faster, because salt and grime do not bond, and stretch the interval between machine polishes. Machine polish — a dual-action polisher on a white hardtop: slow passes, light pressure, the pad kept flat. Gelcoat versus paint Know which one your boat has before anyone picks up a buffer. Gelcoat is typically a quarter to one millimetre thick, nominally half. Light oxidation polishes out; medium needs compound then polish; heavy needs an extra-cut compound and sometimes wet-sanding first. The rule is the least aggressive product that works, because every cut takes gelcoat off and it does not grow back. Most boats need a full polish and wax at least yearly, more in this sun. After a first correction, an annual light cut is the norm. Awlgrip says do not use polishing compounds on its topcoat. Abrasives shorten the finish and void the warranty. Care is Awlwash and a fresh rinse; Awlcare polymer by hand to hold the shine until it is time to repaint. No traditional waxes, which yellow it. Alexseal allows a fresh rinse after every use, a weekly pH-neutral wash, a polymer sealer two or three times a year, and compounding only by an experienced applicator at slow speed. Aggressive buffing removes coating and shortens its life. Do not trap moisture under covers; it bubbles within days. Painted boats are the ones where a cheap detailer does real damage. Paint has one shine; compound through it and the only fix is a repaint. Teak, stainless and clears Teak. Rinse after salt, scrub gently across the grain with a soft or medium brush, deep clean once or twice a season. Two-part acid cleaners at most twice a year and only for a genuine restoration. Never sand as routine: decks are 8 to 10 mm thick with a 4 to 6 mm wearing layer and each sanding removes half a millimetre to a millimetre. Inspect the seams yearly; a full re-caulk is a professional job. Sealers outlast oils; Semco, the sealer several Coomera detailers use, is re-coated every three to six months in high exposure, or when the deck stops beading water. Stainless. Fresh rinse after every use, soap monthly, a polish and protectant every three to six months, and passivation when tea staining starts to show. It is cosmetic, not structural, but it is the first thing a buyer sees. Clears. Fresh water and a soft cloth. The manufacturers list the products that void the warranty: Windex, Rain-X, Pledge, Plexus, Simple Green and anything with ammonia. Stainless — rinsed and wiped every wash; tea-staining polished out before it pits. What it costs No Gold Coast detailer publishes a rate card. Short Marine, Gold Coast Antifouling, Sea Spray Marine, The Boat Butler, Gold Coast Mobile Boat Detailing, GC Marine Services and B&S Detailing all quote on inspection, and the sensible reason is that the condition of the boat decides the price more than her length does. The only Australian published rates are in Sydney. Job, 60 ft in reasonable condition Published rate Works out at Detail wash $5.00 a foot, Sydney about $300 Detail wash and wax plus $3.50 a foot about $510 Machine polish, topsides and machine wax $20 a foot for 51 to 55 ft; custom above about $1,200 and up Full exterior wash and polish, high-end Sydney provider $90 a foot about $5,400 Ceramic coating not published for a 60 ft yacht in Australia ask for the preparation and the coating as separate lines Heavy oxidation, mould, perished clears and gelcoat that needs cutting are quoted separately everywhere. For budgeting, a fortnightly wash on a 60-footer at the Sydney rate is around $7,800 a year, which is the figure in our cost-of-ownership guide. The rules Queensland’s Environmental Protection Act makes everyone responsible for keeping contaminants out of the water and the stormwater. The guidance is to wash where the water is collected and treated, to use water alone where you can, and to choose biodegradable, phosphate-free products. Gold Coast City Marina runs treatment and recycling plants for its wash-down water and holds a Level 3 Clean Marina rating, which is why owners and contractors go through an induction there. In-water hull cleaning needs separate state approval. What to check before you pay for it The quote names the products: soap, compound, polish, wax or coating, by brand. For a cut and polish, the detailer knows whether the hull is gelcoat or paint, and says so. For ceramic, the preparation is priced as its own line, with the days on the hardstand and the aftercare written down. Clears are cleaned with water only, and the detailer can say which products they will never use on them. Teak is cleaned, not sanded, unless you have asked for a restoration. Every visit ends with a report, or at least a photo of anything found. What we do Marine HQ crews wash managed yachts on a schedule, weekly or fortnightly depending on use and berth, with the routine above and a photograph of anything they find, into the owner’s MyYacht app. Cut and polish, teak, stainless and ceramic are scoped into the annual haul-out where the hull is at the right height and out of the sun. If she has gone dull, or you want her kept the way she was delivered, call 0439 748 387 or email yachtsupport@marinehq.com.au.

t: Do you need full-time crew? Driving her yourself, day crew, captains, and what happens when your captain leaves
d: The Queensland rules for an owner at the helm of a 40–120 ft motor yacht, what insurers actually ask, the four ways to run a boat and what each costs, the continuity problem when a captain moves on, and how a support network and the MyYacht app fix it.
x: Can I drive her myself? What your insurer will actually ask The honest limits Four ways to run a yacht When the captain leaves Where Marine HQ comes in MyYacht: the record that lives with the boat Learning to run her yourself What we do Can I drive my own 60 or 70 ft motor yacht in Queensland? Does having paid crew make my yacht a commercial vessel? Will my insurer make me have a captain? What does a full-time captain cost in Australia? What does day crew cost? What actually walks out the door when a captain leaves? The short version: in Queensland you can legally drive any size of private motor yacht on a recreational licence, no Australian insurer publishes a length above which you must have a captain, and a competent couple can run a 60 to 70 ft boat themselves. The longer version is that the law is the easy part. What decides how much crew a yacht needs is how she is used, how she is kept, and what happens to everything her captain knows on the day he hands back the keys. Key facts - The licence — a Queensland recreational marine licence covers any engine over 4.5 kW, any length; the 12 m limit went in 2013 - Commercial or not — paid crew do not make her commercial; charter or hire does, and then AMSA rules apply - Insurance — no published size threshold; policies exclude a skipper without “adequate skill and experience” - The practical line — about 70 ft for an owner-operating couple; beyond 65 to 75 ft the upkeep is a full-time job - Day crew — Gold Coast deckhand $400 a day; freelance captain $350 to $500; relief captain about $1,000 a day - Full-time captain — $100,000 package on a 75 ft; about $113,000 employer cost before leave, flights and relief cover Can I drive her myself? Yes, legally. Queensland requires a marine licence to operate any boat with an engine over 4.5 kW and sets no vessel length or tonnage limit for private recreational use. The old rule that limited new licence holders to boats under 12 m was removed in January 2013. The licence is for life. If your licence is from another state you can boat here on it as long as it is current; once you move to Queensland you have three months to swap it. New South Wales runs the same way in reverse: a Queensland licence is good for three months of NSW boating, and a NSW general boat licence covers any length as long as the use is not commercial. The line that matters is commercial use, and AMSA draws it clearly. A vessel used only for recreation is not a domestic commercial vessel, and AMSA specifically says that paying someone to operate or crew her, or paying an instructor to train you, does not change that. Chartering her, hiring her out, or taking money for a trip does. At that point she needs a certificate of survey, a certificate of operation and a certificated master: Coxswain Grade 1 for vessels under 12 m, Master under 24 m for most yachts in this range, Master under 45 m above that. The local pilotage rules only bite above 50 m, well beyond a 120-footer. Worth knowing Some Gold Coast pages still say boats over 12 m need an “advanced” licence endorsement. That is the pre-2013 rule. Maritime Safety Queensland’s own fact sheet is the source: any length, one licence. At the controls — a wireless remote for close-quarters berthing, and the helm under way. What your insurer will actually ask Every owner-operator question online ends with “your insurer will want a captain”, so it is worth reading what Australian policies say. None of them publish a length or a value above which a professional skipper is compulsory. Club Marine excludes any claim when the boat is under the control of an unlicensed person where a licence is required, or “a person without adequate experience to reasonably control that boat”. Its target market is an owner who “has a boat licence” and “adequate skill and experience to control the insured boat”. Paid skippers and crew in charge of your boat are not covered under your liability section; they need their own. Pantaenius excludes loss while the vessel is controlled by someone “who did not have the necessary experience and training to reasonably and safely control the vessel”, excludes charter unless cover is added, and lists single-handed sailing as an exclusion. Nautilus asks on the proposal form whether you are the normal skipper, how many years you have on cruisers, yachts and catamarans, full details of the usual skipper’s experience and claims, whether you have done a boating course, and what percentage of the boat’s value you spend on maintenance each year. So the assessment is done at application, on your history. Where insurers get cautious is a large jump in size: a first boat at 70 ft, or a step from 45 to 75. The usual answer is not a permanent captain but a period of supervised handling, on your own boat, with someone who does it for a living. On the Gold Coast, the National Maritime College charges $405 for a three-hour session aboard your vessel and $135 an hour after that. The honest limits Owners who run their own boats say roughly the same thing across every forum and magazine. Around 70 ft is the largest boat a couple can manage comfortably as owner-operators. Pods, joystick docking, bow and stern thrusters, station-keeping, remote anchor controls and a set of headsets have pushed that number up a lot in fifteen years; a wireless docking remote for engines, thrusters and anchor costs $5,000 to $20,000 in Australia. Docking is the part that frightens people, and it is the part the technology has solved. Upkeep is the part it has not. Yachting World’s view is that after 60 ft the time spent on upkeep starts to outweigh the enjoyment unless you live aboard. Owners on YachtForums put it more bluntly: a boat over 65 to 75 ft is a full-time job for one person to clean and maintain. A wash-down on a 70-footer is a couple of hours for two people, every week. The engine room, the systems checks, the trades, the paperwork and the yard are on top. That is the real question. Not whether you are allowed to drive her, but who is going to do the other forty hours a week. The other forty hours — the washing, polishing and checking that keep a yacht ready to go. Four ways to run a yacht Model Who drives Who does the upkeep What it costs, published Owner-operated, with management You A management company’s crew on a schedule; trades booked and supervised for you Wash-down crew by the day or the visit; management fee per vessel Owner-operated, day crew You A freelance deckhand on the days you need one Gold Coast listing: $400 a day for a temporary deckhand; freelance deckhands and mates $150 to $500 a day Part-time or relief captain A freelance captain for passages, deliveries and the days you want one You, or day crew, in between Freelance captains $350 to $500 a day; a relief captain on a 32 m was advertised at about $1,000 a day plus flights Full-time captain The captain The captain, plus crew on bigger boats $100,000 package for a junior captain on a 75 ft; $10,000 to $14,000 a month including super on a 100 to 120 ft; about $113,000 employer cost on a $100,000 base after 12% super and WorkCover, before leave, flights, training and four weeks’ relief cover A full-time captain also comes with a five-and-a-half or six-day week, four weeks’ leave that someone has to cover, and a cabin. On a boat under 80 ft that is used some weekends and a few weeks a year, most owners find the first three rows cover it, and the money goes into the boat instead. {{cta}} When the captain leaves Here is the problem nobody writes about from the owner’s side. Industry turnover runs at 20 to 40% a year. A 2023 survey found 40% of captains planning to look for a new boat that year, and only 69% expecting to still be a captain in five years. Replacing a captain-level role is estimated to cost more than 200% of the salary once you count the search, the gap and the mistakes. The expensive part is not the recruitment. It is what leaves with the person: the service history, the known faults and how they are worked around, which contractor to call and which to avoid, the passwords, the way she likes to be brought alongside in a north-easterly, the list of things that were “going to be fixed after the season”. One marine software company describes the new captain’s first month as “digital archaeology”: piecing the boat together from PDFs, spreadsheets and old emails. Another tells the story of an engineer retiring with twenty years of engine history in his head. A proper handover helps. The checklists cover documents, certificates, safety gear status, open defects, logs, accounts, safe codes and passwords, and a five to ten day overlap with maintenance logs handed over in the first 48 hours. But a handover only works if there is something to hand over, and if the next captain leaves in two years you are doing it again. The fix is structural: the record has to live with the boat, not with whoever is running her this season. Where Marine HQ comes in We are the layer that stays. Whether an owner runs the boat themselves, has a captain, or something in between, Marine HQ sits underneath as a support network for the vessel: A team on call. Crew for wash-downs, day work and turnarounds on a schedule or when needed, engineers and trades booked and supervised, someone on the hardstand at the yard. Relief and delivery skippers. When the captain is on leave, when the boat needs moving to Sydney or the Whitsundays, or when an owner wants a professional aboard for a passage. Support for the captain, not competition with them. A good captain gets a maintenance schedule already written, trades already vetted, quotes handled, and a second pair of hands for the jobs a crew of one cannot do alone. Continuity. When a captain leaves, the boat’s record, her schedule, her history and her contacts are all still there. The new captain starts from the boat, not from zero, and the owner does not lose a season. MyYacht: the record that lives with the boat MyYacht is the Marine HQ owner and crew app, and for a team it is the single place the boat’s life is kept. The worklist. Every job on the boat, standard maintenance and boat-specific, with a code, a due date and who it is assigned to. Crew see their own jobs; the owner sees all of them. Jobs, quotes and approvals. A request from the owner or a fault found by crew becomes a job, gets quoted, and is approved in the app before work starts. Photos and progress notes sit on the job. The maintenance schedule. Engine and generator services by hours, antifoul and haul-out by date, safety gear by expiry, so nothing depends on someone remembering. Hours and reporting. Crew clock on and off against a job, submit their day, and the hours flow to the job card. The owner sees what was done and what it cost. Documents and certificates. Registration, insurance, survey, the vessel dossier and the standard operating procedures, with expiry reminders. Where she is and what the weather is doing. Live position and the coastal forecast for wherever she is. Photos with notes. Crew and directors talk on one thread, the owner sees what is shared with them. A captain who joins a Marine HQ boat opens the app and finds three years of history, the open defects, the trades, the schedule and the standard procedures. A captain who leaves takes nothing the boat needs. {{product:programme}} Learning to run her yourself If the plan is to drive her yourself, the Gold Coast is a good place to learn. Own-boat tuition. National Maritime College, based on the Gold Coast, runs three-hour sessions aboard your vessel for $405, with extra hours at $135. Southern Cross Yachting and Paradigm Training at The Boat Works offer own-boat and powerboat courses on enquiry. A commercial ticket, even if you never charter. Coxswain Grade 1 at TAFE Queensland’s Coomera campus is four weeks, $4,645 full fee or $1,665 subsidised, and covers seamanship, navigation and engineering to a standard most owners never otherwise reach. Sea School at Burleigh and Paradigm at Coomera run the same ticket. A stepping-stone boat. The forum advice, repeated by brokers, is to learn on a 40 to 55 ft boat before stepping to 70. Insurers like it too. What we do Marine HQ supports owners at every point on this spectrum on the Gold Coast: crew by the day or on a schedule, relief and delivery skippers, a maintenance and trades team behind whoever is at the helm, and MyYacht holding the boat’s record so that no departure resets it. If you are weighing up a captain, a bigger boat, or running her yourself, call 0439 748 387 or email yachtsupport@marinehq.com.au and we will talk it through with the numbers in front of us.

t: Gold Coast marinas compared: where to keep a 40–120 ft motor yacht
d: Sanctuary Cove, Southport Yacht Club, The Boat Works, GCCM, Hope Harbour, Marina Mirage, Runaway Bay and more, compared on berths, depth, fuel, haul-out, distance to the Seaway and published rates.
x: The comparison at a glance Sanctuary Cove Marina Southport Yacht Club Marina, Main Beach The Boat Works, Coomera Gold Coast City Marina & Shipyard (GCCM), Coomera Hope Harbour Marina, Hope Island Marina Mirage, Main Beach Runaway Bay Marina Pacific Point Marina (formerly Horizon Shores), Steiglitz The smaller and newer options Getting up the river Cyclone season How to choose What we do Which Gold Coast marina is closest to open water? How much does a marina berth cost on the Gold Coast? Can I live aboard at a Gold Coast marina? Is the Coomera River deep enough for a 60 or 70 ft motor yacht? What is the speed limit on the Coomera River? Where do Gold Coast yachts go in a cyclone? The Gold Coast has eleven commercial marinas and about 170 superyacht berths, more than anywhere else in Australia, so the question is rarely whether there is a berth. It is which one. The honest split is Broadwater marinas at Main Beach and Runaway Bay, five minutes from the Seaway and priced accordingly, versus Coomera River marinas an hour and a half upstream at six knots, next to the shipyards and out of the weather. Key facts - Closest to open water — Marina Mirage and Southport Yacht Club (about 5 minutes to the Seaway); Runaway Bay (2 nautical miles) - Closest to the trades — The Boat Works and Gold Coast City Marina, in the Coomera precinct with 300-tonne lifts on site - Only published rate card — Southport Yacht Club, effective 1 May 2026; everyone else quotes on enquiry - Speed limit — 6 knots from Paradise Point all the way up the Coomera River - Channel depth — about 3.0 m at Sanctuary Cove and GCCM; 3.5 m at The Boat Works at low tide - New in 2026 — Mantaray Marina at The Spit (opened August); Main Beach Superyacht Marina under construction The comparison at a glance Eleven marinas on one map. Marine HQ works from both Coomera yards, The Boat Works and Gold Coast City Marina, numbers 3 and 4 in orange. Tap a number for the name. {{map:gold-coast-marinas}} Marina Where Berths Max vessel Fuel on site Haul-out on site To the Seaway Rates Sanctuary Cove Hope Island, Coomera River 300–480 65 m 24/7, 120 L/min diesel No not published; Hope Island next door says 40 min Enquiry Southport Yacht Club Main Beach 300 130 m 24-hour wharf 35–40 t lift, to 55 ft about 5 min Published, May 2026 The Boat Works Coomera 125–150 in water 50 m berths, 75 m alongside Yes, plus bunkering 300 t, 100 t, 70 t lifts 11 nm Enquiry Gold Coast City Marina (GCCM) Coomera 200 75 m 24/7 tap-and-go 300 t and 50 t lifts about 1.5 h at 6 kn Schedule from Nov 2022 Hope Harbour Hope Island 280 40 m Yes No 15 min Enquiry Marina Mirage Main Beach 76–78 70 m+ No, next door at SYC No about 5 min Enquiry Runaway Bay Runaway Bay 195 wet, 260 dry 30 m Yes 35 t lift, to 16 m 2 nm Enquiry Pacific Point (was Horizon Shores) Steiglitz 550+ 40 m 24/7 70 t lift Southern Moreton Bay, not the Broadwater Enquiry Hope Island Marina Hope Island about 240 30 m Yes No about 40 min Rentals from $1,050/month Mantaray The Spit 67 60 m Yes No at the Seaway Leases from $2,000/month Berth counts move with each expansion and sources disagree by a few dozen; the figures are the marinas’ own where they publish them. Sanctuary Cove Marina The resort marina, and the address most people picture. Sanctuary Cove is a Platinum Gold Anchor, Superyacht Ready marina and was Marina of the Year in 2023. It takes vessels to 65 m with a 3.0 m draught and 15 m beam, and its J Pier expansion added ten 30 m and fifteen 18 m berths, bringing it to 63 superyacht-capable berths. The fuel jetty runs 24/7 on card swipe with fast-flow diesel at 120 litres a minute and bulk pricing on fills over 1,000 litres. Fob access to berths and amenities is 24 hours, with CCTV and patrols, three-phase power, laundry, private showers, Wi-Fi and a helipad. What it does not have is a yard. Sanctuary Cove markets its proximity to the Coomera precinct for refit work, which in practice means a short run upriver to The Boat Works or GCCM for every haul-out. It also does not publish rates or a live-aboard policy; berthing is by enquiry for casual, permanent and superyacht categories. Southport Yacht Club Marina, Main Beach The only Gold Coast marina with a public rate card, and the one to benchmark everything else against. Three hundred berths, vessels to 130 m, power to 600 amps, an official Customs clearance port and Australia’s largest floating superyacht berth at 160 m. Five minutes from the Seaway, with a 24-hour self-serve fuel wharf and a hardstand with a 35 to 40 tonne travel lift for boats up to 55 ft. On site: the Waterfront Restaurant, the Bosun’s Locker chandlery, a members’ gym, laundry and pump-out. The 1 May 2026 rates, including GST, per month: Berth Gold Member Visitor 49 ft / 15 m double $1,186 $1,930 59 ft / 18 m single $2,064 $3,145 66 ft / 20 m single or T-head $2,598 $3,380 73 ft / 22 m single $3,174 $4,013 82 ft / 25 m single $4,122 $5,500 Over 82 ft / 25 m on application on application Wide and catamaran berths cost more (a 59 ft cat is $2,682 member, $4,430 visitor), three-phase power is 35 cents a kilowatt hour, and a 12-month contract on the 59 ft single is $19,311 for members. There is a waiting list for permanent berths, reported at around 300 vessels, and the club is adding 19 berths. The Boat Works, Coomera One of Marine HQ’s two bases. A working marina inside a 55-acre shipyard, and the biggest lifting capacity in the city: a 300-tonne Marine Travelift, a 100-tonne and a 70-tonne lift, plus a 45-tonne hydraulic lift for wide catamarans. The South Marina has 125 work berths, with around 150 in-water service berths and 300 hardstand allocations across the site, and 15 superyacht berths to 50 m with a 75 m alongside berth. Water is 3.5 m at low tide, maintained by dredging. It is about 11 nautical miles from the Seaway. The Boat Works is where you go to get things done: 80 to 90 marine trade tenants, owner-operated work allowed at no extra charge, a bunkering dock, pump-out, 24/7 CCTV with on-site caretakers, live-aboard ensuites, a hardstand area for up to 16 live-aboard boats, courtesy cars, an owners’ lounge and three places to eat. It earned 5 Gold Anchors and Superyacht Ready status in 2023, and during Cyclone Alfred in March 2025 it secured about 400 vessels with no damage. Rates are not published. Gold Coast City Marina & Shipyard (GCCM), Coomera Marine HQ’s other base, and the other half of the Coomera precinct. GCCM, operated by d’Albora, has 200 berths for vessels of 10 to 75 m, on-water service berths to 75 m, 24-hour security with site-wide CCTV, three-phase power to 125 amps and a 24/7 tap-and-go fuel wharf with bunkering on request. The shipyard runs 50-tonne and 300-tonne lifts, 50,000 m² of hardstand, sheds from 8 to 45 m, 300 dry-stack spaces and more than 90 businesses. It was the first shipyard in the Asia-Pacific to receive 5 Gold Anchors and took Marina of the Year, Boatyard of the Year and Dry Stack Facility of the Year at the 2025 industry awards. GCCM’s last published berth schedule is from November 2022, marked as subject to change and excluding utilities: 51–60 ft $1,650 a month, 61–70 ft $1,925, 71–80 ft $2,400, 81–90 ft $3,200, 91–100 ft $5,000 and 101–110 ft $6,000, with vessels over 111 ft at $2.30 a foot a day on a monthly stay. Multihulls pay 1.5 times on a T-head and double in a berth. Freehold berths also change hands here; a 16 m berth on Pier H listed with annual outgoings of $4,245. Hope Harbour Marina, Hope Island The first marina upstream after Paradise Point and, at its own estimate, 15 minutes from the Seaway. Its 280 berths take vessels from 6 to 40 m including multihulls, on composite pontoons in a basin branched off the river, which keeps it out of the tidal flow and is why it is marketed as cyclone and flood shelter. Fuel jetty with premium unleaded and diesel, 24/7 CCTV with on-site guards, chandlery, café, laundry, tender service, boat ramp and three-phase power on the larger berths, with the Ramada hotel, Marlin bar, pool and tennis courts alongside. No yard. Rates are by application. Marina Mirage, Main Beach Seventy-six to seventy-eight deep-water berths from 12 m to 70 m and beyond, 3.5 to 4 m at the berth, five minutes from the Seaway and next door to Southport Yacht Club’s fuel wharf, since Mirage has none of its own. Power from 15 to 250 amps, a helipad, 24-hour security with key-fob gates, undercover parking and the La Luna floating beach club. The rebuilt marina reopened in 2021 and took Marina of the Year (under 140 boats) in 2023. The big news is the $500 million Makris redevelopment: the retail precinct closed in November 2025, a 126-room Luxury Collection resort and 38 residences are on the way for 2029, and the marina is to keep operating through construction. Rates not published. Runaway Bay Marina Two nautical miles from the Seaway with 195 wet berths for 8 to 30 m vessels and 260 dry-stack spaces to 10 m, a fuel dock, a 35-tonne travel lift for boats to 16 m, and a good cluster of trades on site including Short Marine and Gold Coast Antifouling. Security is 24/7 CCTV with on-site guards. Staying aboard for a night or two is allowed at no charge; full-time live-aboard is not offered. Quote form only for rates. Pacific Point Marina (formerly Horizon Shores), Steiglitz Now a d’Albora marina and renamed. More than 550 wet berths for vessels to 40 m, 330 dry-storage spaces, a 70-tonne travel lift, refit sheds, 24/7 fuel, a chandlery seven days a week and after-hours patrols. It sits on southern Moreton Bay near Jacobs Well rather than on the Broadwater, which suits owners heading north to Moreton Bay more than those running out the Seaway. Live-aboard is permitted subject to conditions. Steiglitz Reach to the entrance is a 6-knot zone. {{cta}} The smaller and newer options Hope Island Marina , on the Coomera River next to Sanctuary Cove: berths 12 to 30 m for monohulls and cats, about 40 minutes from the Seaway. Coomera Waters Marina , Coomera River North Branch: 70 berths, 12 to 20 m, permanent and casual. Sovereign Island Marina , Paradise Point: 30 berths, 10 to 45 m, digital gates and 24/7 CCTV; $10 million public liability cover required. Mantaray Marina , The Spit: 67 berths from 10 to 60 m, twenty of them superyacht berths, bookings from April 2026 and officially open 1 August 2026. Monthly leases advertised from $2,000. Main Beach Superyacht Marina , the old Mariner’s Cove: 66 berths to 73 m with high-flow fuel, a captain’s lounge and a helipad, alongside a Ritz-Carlton due 2029. The marina was targeted for the third quarter of 2026. Getting up the river The Seaway is 250 m wide with a permanent sand bypass, dredged to a minimum of about 4.5 m outside and 4.8 m inside. It is described as the safest bar in south-east Queensland, but on an ebb tide against a south-easterly swell it is not a place to be casual. Cross on the flood or at high slack, keep clear of the shallow bank north-east of the heads and log on with Seaway Tower or VMR Southport on VHF 16 or 73. Entrance dredging was under way in August 2026 and the sand-bypass jetty is closed to the public until the end of the year. Larger yachts go up on a rising tide and aim to arrive about an hour and a half before high water; the tide at Paradise Point runs about an hour behind the Seaway. Take the southern arm around Coomera Island. Worth knowing Guideline limits for the run from the Seaway to the Coomera precinct without a pilot are 60 m and a 2.1 m draught; to Southport Yacht Club, 65 m and 3 m. The Coomera River marinas came through it as the region’s storm shelter: The Boat Works hauled 275 boats and secured 125 in the water without a scratch, and Hope Harbour’s off-river basin did what it was built for. t: Yacht SOPs: what standard operating procedures are, why they pay for themselves, and what a good set includes
d: What an SOP is on a private motor yacht, why checklists work, which procedures every yacht should have written down, how they help with crew changes, insurance and resale, and how Marine HQ writes them and puts them on your phone.
x: Why a checklist works What goes wrong without them What the law says The SOPs every motor yacht should have What a good SOP looks like How SOPs help beyond the dock How Marine HQ writes them In the app, on your phone What we do What is an SOP on a yacht? Does a private yacht legally need SOPs? Which SOPs should every motor yacht have? How long should an SOP be? Do SOPs help with insurance or resale? Can I just buy a template? An SOP, a Standard Operating Procedure, is the written way a job is done on your yacht. Not how a generator works in general, but how this generator is started on this boat, in what order, with which breakers, and what to check before you walk away. A commercial vessel has to have them. A private yacht does not, and most do not, which is why so much of what a yacht knows lives in one person’s head. Here is what they are, why they work, which ones matter, and how we write them. Key facts - What it is — one or two pages: the steps in order, the limits, and a checklist, written for one yacht - Required? — for commercial vessels, yes, under Marine Order 504; for a private yacht, no - Why bother — the boat runs the same way whoever is aboard, and nothing depends on memory - Start with — pre-departure and stand-down, then anchoring, tender, fuelling, power changeover and emergencies - Where they live — in print aboard, and on your phone in the MyYacht app - Ready-made — the three everyday checklists are $7; anything specific to your yacht is written for her Why a checklist works The best evidence comes from surgery. In 2009 a World Health Organization study across eight hospitals introduced a 19-item checklist read aloud before, during and after an operation. Major complications fell from 11% to 7% of patients, and deaths from 1.5% to 0.8%. Nothing about the surgeons’ skill changed. What changed was that the routine steps stopped depending on memory, and that everyone in the room knew the plan. Aviation has worked this way for decades, and the lesson transfers directly to a yacht. The people who run boats well are not the ones who remember everything. They are the ones who do not have to. What goes wrong without them The seacock left open, the shore power left off, the hatch left ajar. Most damage at the dock is something left on, left open or left unrecorded after a trip. Two people, two methods. The owner anchors one way, the weekend skipper another, and the windlass pays for the difference. The guest brief that never happens. Life jackets, the raft, the fire blanket, and which door not to open under way. The captain who leaves. Yacht crew turnover runs at 20 to 40% a year, and a 2023 survey found 40% of captains planning to look for a new boat. A proper handover is meant to include the equipment lists, the procedures for critical equipment, the maintenance history and the open defects. If none of that is written down, there is nothing to hand over. What the law says A domestic commercial vessel in Australia must operate under a safety management system. Marine Order 504, revised from 1 June 2025, requires documented procedures for onboard operations and emergencies, crew training and drills, and clear roles and responsibilities. That is the standard a charter yacht works to. A recreational yacht is outside that system. AMSA is specific that paying someone to operate or crew her does not make her commercial. So a private owner has no obligation to write anything down, which is exactly why the well-run private yachts borrow the commercial habit. Worth knowing If there is any chance your yacht will go into charter, the procedures are the first thing the safety management system needs. Writing them while she is private is far easier than writing them the month before survey. The SOPs every motor yacht should have Procedure When it is used What it prevents Pre-departure Every trip Leaving with a fault you could have found at the dock Stand-down Every trip Flat batteries, flooded bilges, an unlocked boat Anchoring and anchor retrieval Every night at anchor Windlass damage, a fouled anchor, dragging Tender launch and recovery Every day at anchor Davit and crane overloads, crushed fingers Fuelling Every fill Spills, the wrong tank, static and fumes Shore power and generator changeover Every arrival and departure Tripped supplies, damaged inverters and chargers Guest safety brief Every new guest The questions nobody asks until it matters Fire, flooding, person overboard Hopefully never Losing the first two minutes Storm and cyclone preparation Each season A scramble when a warning is issued Her own specials As fitted Stabilisers, passerelle, watermaker, tender garage The first two are the same on almost every motor yacht. Everything below them depends on her equipment, which is why a template only gets you so far. {{product:checklists}} What a good SOP looks like A header that says which boat and which equipment. Vessel, the system it covers, the date and who wrote it. The purpose in one line. What the procedure is for and when it is used. The limits. Wind, depth, load, engine state: the conditions under which you do not do this. The steps, in the order you do them. Short lines, one action each, using the names on her own switches and valves. The warnings where they apply. Next to the step, not in a paragraph at the end. A checklist. The same steps as tick boxes, for the day you are doing it rather than learning it. What to do when it does not work. The windlass will not retrieve; the generator will not take the load. One or two pages. If it is longer, it is a manual, and it will stay in the drawer. {{cta}} How SOPs help beyond the dock Crew changes. A new captain or a relief skipper reads the procedures and runs her the way she has always been run. The owner does not spend a season re-teaching the boat. Insurance. No Australian policy asks for SOPs by name. But they exclude claims when the boat is under the control of someone without adequate experience to control her, and the proposal form asks about your experience, any boating course, and how the boat is maintained. A yacht with written procedures and a schedule is an easier story to tell an underwriter, and an easier one to tell after an incident. Resale. A buyer is paying for the boat and for the evidence that she was looked after. A bound set of procedures, the maintenance schedule and the records is what a surveyor asks to see. Family and guests. The person most likely to be at the helm when you are not is someone who knows the boat less well than you do. How Marine HQ writes them We write SOPs aboard, with whoever runs the yacht, because the detail that matters is in her own equipment: which breaker, which valve, which side the passerelle stows. Each one follows the structure above and is checked by running it. Most owners take them as part of the Vessel Dossier , the bound record we produce for a yacht: her particulars, an emergency response card, a safety checklist, a tailored maintenance schedule, an insurance summary, a compliance register and contacts, with pre-departure and one further procedure of your choice, in print and digital. Further SOPs are added singly or in sets, and the whole set is reviewed each year. It is quoted per yacht. In the app, on your phone A procedure in a folder is used once. A procedure on the phone in your pocket is used every trip. On a Marine HQ yacht the pre-departure and stand-down checklists live in the MyYacht app: tick as you go, progress is saved on the device, and anything not fitted to your yacht can be skipped. The full written SOPs sit under Documents, with the dossier and the certificates, and open in the app. Checklists — pre-departure and stand-down, ticked on the phone. Shown on our demonstration yacht. Documents — the written SOPs sit with the dossier and certificates. What we do If you run her yourself, start with the three everyday checklists. If you want procedures written for your yacht, or a full Vessel Dossier, call 0439 748 387 or email yachtsupport@marinehq.com.au and tell us what she is and how you use her. We will tell you which procedures she needs and write them aboard.

t: Sanctuary Cove International Boat Show 2027: dates, what's there, and how to get the most out of it
d: SCIBS runs 20 to 23 May 2027 at Sanctuary Cove. What last year's show looked like, how to plan a visit, how buying at the show really works, and what Marine HQ did on the docks in 2026.
x: What last year's show looked like What is actually there Planning a day that is worth it Buying at the show What we did at the show in 2026 What we do When is the Sanctuary Cove boat show in 2027? How much are tickets? Where do I park? Which day is best? Can I sea-trial a boat at the show? Are show discounts real? The Sanctuary Cove International Boat Show is the biggest on-water show in the southern hemisphere, and it happens on our doorstep. The 38th show runs Thursday 20 to Sunday 23 May 2027 at Sanctuary Cove on Hope Island. If you own a motor yacht on the Gold Coast, or you are about to, it is the four days a year when every builder, broker, engine dealer and trade is in one place. Here is what last year looked like, how to plan a day that is worth the ticket, and how buying at the show really works. Key facts — SCIBS 2027 - Dates — 20 to 23 May 2027, Thursday to Sunday, 9am to 5pm each day - Where — Sanctuary Cove Marina, Masthead Way, Hope Island, about 45 minutes south of Brisbane - Tickets — online only, no gate sales; 2026 adults were $31.50 early and $42 later, under-16s free - Scale in 2026 — 41,000 visitors, 300-plus exhibitors, 800-plus boats, 70-plus launches, over $400 million in sales and orders - Getting there — no public parking on site; park-and-ride coaches, shuttle from Helensvale station, ferry from Hope Harbour - Best days — Thursday and Friday if you want time aboard; weekends fill from about 11am What last year’s show looked like 41,000+ visitors over four days, 2026 800+ boats, about 400 of them on the water $400m+ exhibitor sales and orders, Griffith University estimate 28 m the largest boat at the show, a Horizon FD90 The 2026 show sold out its exhibition space and its hospitality zones, and put 300-plus exhibitors and more than 800 boats on a marina that had just been expanded to 346 berths for the event. Griffith University put exhibitor sales and orders above $400 million, with 9,383 interstate and overseas visitors from 28 countries and a quarter of visitors extending their stay in Queensland. For a motor-yacht buyer, the interesting part was the water. Horizon brought a $100 million fleet to Pier G, including the global debut of the ES88. Riviera ran twelve yachts from 39 to 78 ft down the Coomera River in convoy the Tuesday before, headlined by the world premiere of the 6200 Sport Yacht. Maritimo launched the S50 Sedan and two new Caribbeans and had 1,400 people register to inspect. Princess brought seven boats, its largest showing in the southern hemisphere, and Sunseeker, Palm Beach, Grand Banks, Whitehaven, Axopar and Sirena all had premieres. Sailfish sold more than $2 million of catamarans and openly listed a $3.4 million boat at a $700,000 show discount, which tells you show pricing is real. The 2025 show, for comparison, drew 45,865 visitors and 824 boats, 422 of them on the water, with 92 launches. The show has run every year since 1989, when Sanctuary Cove was four years old and the event was called the Queensland International Boat Show. What is actually there The Marina. Superyachts, production motor yachts, sailing yachts and multihulls up to 165 ft, on a marina that now has 63 superyacht-capable berths. This is where a 40 to 120 ft buyer spends the day. The Pavilion and Marina Village streets. Trailer boats, outboards, tenders, jet skis and engines, plus the booths at the entrance. The Sports, Leisure and Fishing Precinct. Twenty thousand square metres of gear, demos and masterclasses, with a fishing programme running 10am to 3.30pm. Sea Trial Zone, C Pier. Test rides on smaller powerboats and tenders. Larger yachts are trialled by arrangement with the dealer. Talks and seminars on ownership, safety and navigation, and Riviera’s own Owners’ Festival of Boating with more than 30 sessions during show week. Lagoon Beach Club. The hospitality precinct, Thursday to Saturday, from a $129 brunch to a $290 full day, admission included. The trades. Gold Coast City Marina and The Boat Works both exhibit with their on-site trade partners, and The Boat Works runs an out-of-water used-boat show at Coomera during the same week, twenty minutes away by car. Show week — the Coomera precinct is a ten-minute boat ride from the show, and both yards are busiest in the weeks before it. Planning a day that is worth it Book tickets online before you go. There is no box office at the gate. Under-16s are free. Pick Thursday or Friday if you are serious. Same boats, same hours, half the crowd. Save the weekend for the family. Book appointments a week out. Email the dealers for the two or three boats you actually want to see and ask for a time aboard. Boats with a queue do not open their engine rooms for walk-ups. Mark up the map. The marina is bigger than it looks. Start on the water in the morning, land displays after lunch. Dress for boarding. Slip-on shoes with grip, because shoes come off on every boat, plus a hat, sunscreen and water. There is little shade on the piers. Photograph the spec and price board on every boat you step aboard. By 3pm they blur together. Ask to open the engine room on any boat you are considering. How easy that is to do tells you how easy she will be to own. Leave the Coomera River clear. The marina is closed to visiting boats during the show. Come by road or ferry. {{cta}} Buying at the show Show incentives come from the builder to the dealer, and they are usually real: a sharper price, a service or accessories package, or a delivery slot. Three things to hold onto. You are not obliged to sign at the show. Ask what the price is the following week. Compare dealers on the day; come back tomorrow. Get finance and insurance pre-approved before you go. Then a deposit is a decision, not a scramble. The show does not replace the survey and the sea trial. A deposit that is refundable subject to survey and sea trial is normal. A deposit that is not, is not. Before the deposit, get answers to the questions that decide what she costs to own, not just what she costs to buy: the engine and generator service intervals and what the 1,000-hour service involves, the antifoul interval and where she will be lifted, what the berth will cost, and whether the builder’s warranty work happens here or in Sydney. Our cost-of-ownership guide has the Gold Coast numbers, and our marinas guide has the berths. Worth knowing The two days before the show, the Australian marine industry holds its ASMEX conference on the Gold Coast, and the yards at Coomera are at their busiest in the weeks leading in. If your own boat needs a haul-out around May, book it for March or April, or for June when the yards run their winter specials. {{product:calculator}} What we did at the show in 2026 Marine HQ spent the four days on the docks with a camera and a question list rather than a stand. We called it Dock Talk: short interviews with three groups of people, for our Instagram and for us. Owners. What is the hardest part of owning a boat, do you use her as much as you would like, who looks after her when you are not aboard, and, the one everyone laughed at first, what is your honest annual running cost. People in the market. First boat or not, what is the biggest concern about taking the leap, what size are you looking at and has that changed since you started shopping, and have you thought about who will manage her when you are not using her. The trades and brokers. The one question every buyer should ask but never does, the biggest mistake first-time buyers make, the true annual cost, and the one piece of electronics a new owner should invest in first. The interview we will remember was with Audrey Greenwood of Flagship International Yacht Brokers, Australia’s first female yacht broker, who founded her own brokerage in Noosa at 25 in the late 1980s and now leads Flagship’s Queensland office at Gold Coast City Marina, on how she got into the industry and what she tells buyers now. Two of our thirteen-year-olds ran a junior reporter edition, which produced better answers than the adults’ questions did. Several of the answers turned into the guides on this site: the cost figures, the marina comparison and the haul-out checklist came straight from what owners on the docks said they wished someone had told them. We will be back in 2027 with the same camera and a longer list. What we do If you are going to the show to buy, we will come with you and look at the boat the way a manager does: engine room access, service history, running gear, systems, and what she will cost to keep here on the Gold Coast. If you are going as an owner, we will meet you on the docks. Call 0439 748 387 or email yachtsupport@marinehq.com.au, and follow @marinehq for Dock Talk.
